Disabled or profile-denied tools are not made available by discovery. ## Troubleshooting - If an external tool is not found, check its app in [Settings Apps](/docs/settings/apps), its Custom Tool or channel configuration, and the active Agent Profile. - If a direct tool worked previously but discovery does not select it, use a precise prompt and inspect Row-Bot Status for effective tool groups. - If a provider rejects tool schemas, choose a compatible tool-capable model or temporarily test eager mode. - If retrieval is noisy, change compression mode or disable unnecessary search tools. For the full runtime model, see [Progressive Tools And Skills](/docs/guides/progressive-tools-and-skills).

## Settings: Skills

Route: /docs/settings/skills

Find, add, try, update, and remove skills, and open the skill editor to create or edit one.

# Settings: Skills Skills are instruction packs that teach Row-Bot how to approach a kind of work. **Settings Skills** works like [Settings Apps](/docs/settings/apps): one library to find skills and one page per skill. ## Where To Find It Open **Settings**, then choose **Skills** in the **Capabilities** group, or search for it with **Find a setting**. The command palette's **Add a skill** opens it too. ## Find A Skill Search by name or by the job, such as "pdf". Search is instant and local; nothing you type leaves this computer. **Search online catalogs** also asks the live catalogs, such as ClawHub, and sends them your search words. The page lists **Your skills** first, then **Featured** and **All skills**. **Add from link or file** adds a skill from a skill page, a GitHub repository, or a .zip or .skill file; nothing is fetched until you agree on the skill's page. ## The Skill Page - **Use it in chat with /_name_** shows the slash command that loads it. - **Settings** says whether chats use it ("Available in every chat without a profile." or "Turned off: chats don't use it.") and which agent profiles include it. To change which profiles use a skill, edit the profile's skills; see [Profiles, Goals, And Agents](/docs/profiles-goals-agents/). - **What's inside** (collapsed) lists its files and scripts, for example "6 files - 1 script", and marks each script. Scripts never run when you add a skill; if Row-Bot runs one later, your approval rules apply. - **Try it** opens a new chat with a draft that uses the skill. The draft stays in the composer; nothing is sent until you send it. - The **** menu has **Turn off**, **Advanced settings**, **Check for updates** for a skill from a catalog, and **Remove...** for a skill you added or created. ## Add A Skill **Add** opens **Add _skill_**, which says where it downloads from and that it "Adds the skill and turns it on". Agree, and Row-Bot checks the skill's files and adds it. Scripts inside a skill never run when it is added. A skill changes instructions only. It does not add credentials, grant tools that an agent profile denies, or skip approvals. ## Use A Skill In Chat Type `/` in a chat and choose the skill from the **Skills** group. Chosen in an empty message, it turns the skill on for the whole chat; chosen inside a message, it focuses only that turn on it. See [Mention an app or a skill](/docs/chat/#mention-an-app-or-a-skill). ## Turn Off Or Remove A Skill - ** Turn off** stops chats using the skill and keeps it; **Turn on** brings it back. - ** Remove...** deletes the skill's files from this computer. Skills built into Row-Bot can be turned off but not removed, and a skill that came with a package is turned off or removed with its package. ## Create Or Edit A Skill **Create a skill** opens the skill editor for a new skill. On a skill's page, ** Advanced settings** opens the editor for that one skill, where you edit it, pin it, and review proposed changes to it. ## Old Links Old links to the Skills section of the former Integrations page open this page. ## Control-Level Reference The [generated Settings Controls reference](/docs/reference/generated/settings-controls#skills-controls) lists every searchable setting on this page. How Row-Bot picks skills automatically is in [Progressive Tools And Skills](/docs/guides/progressive-tools-and-skills), and writing good skills is in [Skills](/docs/skills/). ## Troubleshooting - If a skill is never used, check that it is in **Your skills**, try it with **/_name_**, and make your request match its purpose. - If a skill is used too eagerly, edit it with clearer boundaries or remove it.

## Settings: Apps

Route: /docs/settings/apps

Find and connect the services Row-Bot can work in, including your accounts and messaging channels, choose what each app may do, change its settings, and turn apps off or remove them.

# Settings: Apps Apps are the services Row-Bot can work in, such as Notion, GitHub or a tool that runs on this computer. Your GitHub, Google and X accounts, the Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack and SMS channels, and the tools that use your own key are apps too. **Settings Apps** is where you find them, connect them, choose what each one may do, change their settings, and turn them off or remove them. ## Where To Find It Open **Settings**, then choose **Apps** in the **Connections** group, or search for it with **Find a setting**. The command palette's **Connect an app** opens it too, and requests such as "connect google" or "connect telegram" open that app's page. In a chat, **+ Apps Find more apps** opens it; see [Apps in a chat](/docs/chat/#apps-in-a-chat). ## Find An App Search by an app's name or by what you want done, such as "send email" or "take meeting notes". Search is instant and local: Row-Bot searches catalog copies kept on this computer, and nothing you type leaves it. **Search online catalogs** also asks the live catalogs, such as Hermes, and sends them your search words. The page lists: - **Your apps**: the apps you have added, with anything that needs attention first. Each shows its status: **Ready**, **Off**, **Sign in needed**, **Key needed**, **Finish setup**, **Working...**, **Needs attention**, or **Removed** for a package whose saved data was kept. [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/#apps-and-skills) says what to do about each. - **Featured**, then category chips (Productivity, Developer, Data, Design, Communication, Finance and Local tools), then **All apps**. **Communication** lists the messaging channels. While the app catalog is first being built, the page says **Preparing the app catalog...** and more apps appear in a moment. Each app appears once in results; its other ways to connect are on its page. Apps from their own vendors and from Row-Bot come first, then **More from the community**. Listings that look like placeholders, staging copies or duplicates are left out; **Show all results** shows them too. Each card shows the app's logo, its name and what it does, and who publishes it: - **by _Vendor_** with a check: the service's own vendor publishes it, which Row-Bot confirms by rule, never from a listing's name. - **Built in**: it comes with Row-Bot. - **Community - _publisher_**: anyone else. Check who publishes it and its source on its page before you connect it. A card also says how the app connects: **Hosted - Sign-in**, **API key**, **Hosted** or **Runs on this computer**. Package entries from the Hermes catalog say **Checked when you add**; one made for the Hermes app itself can't be added, and its page says why. Logos come only from Row-Bot or its saved copies; browsing never downloads them, and a letter stands in until a logo is ready. ## The App Page Open an app to see its page (for example `/settings/apps/notion`). The header shows its logo, name, publisher and status, one main action, and a **** menu. The main action is whatever comes next: **Connect**, **Add**, **Set up**, **Sign in**, **Sign in again**, **Add key**, **Continue setup**, **Turn on**, **Fix**, **Retry**, **Try it** or **Delete saved data**. **Try it** opens a new chat with a draft that uses the app; nothing is sent until you send it. The **** menu holds what applies of **Turn off**, **Check for updates** (for a package from GitHub), **Advanced settings** and **Remove...**; for a built-in way to connect it holds **Open its settings**. - **Overview**: what it does, things to ask, and where your data goes. - **Access**: what it may do, grouped as **Looks things up**, **Makes changes** and **Always asks first**, with a count and the choice, such as "8 of 12 actions on - Ask before changes", and **Choose** to change it. See [Choose what an app can do](#choose-what-an-app-can-do). - **Show views in chat**: for an app that can show its results as an interactive view. See [App views](/docs/chat/#app-views). - **Settings**: for a connected app, the account, whether a key is saved (in your system keychain), each setting, and anything it needs on this computer, with **Change settings**. See [Change settings after setup](#change-settings-after-setup). For a built-in way, **Set up** or **Open** opens its own settings. - **Ways to connect**: when an app can be connected more than one way, every way, the recommended one first. See [Ways to connect](#ways-to-connect). - **Included**: for a package, the apps and skills it brought. Each of those says **Installed as part of _package_**. - **Details**: source, version, licence, other catalogs it is listed in, and its identifier. ## Ways To Connect Some apps can be connected in more than one way: through a server the service hosts, through a server that runs on this computer, or through a way built into Row-Bot. The app's page lists them under **Ways to connect**, the recommended one first and marked **Recommended**. Each way says how it connects (**Built in**, **Hosted - Sign-in**, **Hosted - API key**, **Hosted** or **Runs on this computer**) and who publishes it; the one you are looking at says **This one**. Choose another way to open its page. For example: - **GitHub**: GitHub's hosted server (with a token, or with your own OAuth app), then the GitHub account built into Row-Bot, then GitHub's server on this computer. - **Google**: the Google account built into Row-Bot first. - **Slack**: Slack's hosted server, then the Slack channel built into Row-Bot. - **Tavily**: Row-Bot's built-in **Web search** with your Tavily key, then Tavily's hosted server, then its server on this computer. Each way keeps its own credentials. A GitHub account token and a GitHub server connection, for example, never share a token: connecting one doesn't sign in the other. ## Built-In Ways To Connect Some ways to connect are part of Row-Bot itself, so their cards and pages say **Built in**: - the **GitHub**, **Google** and **X** accounts; - the **Telegram**, **WhatsApp**, **Discord**, **Slack** and **Text messages** (SMS) channels; - tools that use your own key: **Web search** (a Tavily key) and **Wolfram Alpha**. A built-in way is set up and changed in its own settings, not with a setup sheet. Its **Set up** (or **Open** once it is set up), and ** Open its settings**, open those settings for that one account, channel or tool only, with **Back** to the app page: - an account opens its step-by-step guide, **Check**, **Reconnect** and **Disconnect**, and what Row-Bot may do with it. See [Accounts And Authorisation](/docs/integrations/accounts). - a channel opens its connect steps, **Start** and **Stop**, pairing and paired accounts. See [Channels](/docs/integrations/channels). - a key tool opens its switch and its key, which stays in your system keychain. Old links to the Accounts and Channels settings pages open the matching app, for example **Apps Google** or **Apps Telegram**. ## Connect An App 1. Choose the main action. A sheet named after it, such as **Connect Notion**, lists what will happen: where requests go, whether you sign in in your browser or paste a key, anything Row-Bot needs to download, and that apps get turned on. **How Row-Bot keeps this safe** explains the protections. 2. Agree, and Row-Bot does the setup itself, showing each step as it goes. 3. It pauses only when it needs you: to sign in (your browser opens), to add a key or a setting, to check what it will install, to open a program, or to choose what the app can do. 4. Choose access on **Here's what _app_ can do**, and the app is ready. ### What A Setup Can Ask For - **Add your key** or **Add your settings**: a key or token is kept in your system keychain; a setting such as a workspace, region or folder is saved with the app. **Where do I get this?** opens the service's own page for it. Optional settings can be left empty. - **Sign in to _app_**: when Row-Bot first connects, it checks whether the service asks you to sign in, so an app whose listing doesn't say can still sign in. Row-Bot signs in through your browser with its own published details, or registers itself with the service. A few services, such as GitHub, accept only your own OAuth app: Row-Bot asks for its **Client ID** and, if it has one, **Client secret (optional)**, both kept in the keychain, and shows the callback address to register, `http://127.0.0.1/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback`. If a sign-in expires and can't be renewed, the app says **Sign in needed**. - **Get ready to run _app_** and **Install what _app_ needs**: an app that runs on this computer may need Node.js or uv, which Row-Bot sets up for its own use, and an npm package, Python package, container image or bundle, which is installed into its own folder, never system-wide. Before anything installs, Row-Bot shows **Exactly what will be installed**: each package's exact version and checksum, checked again when it installs. Install scripts never run. Python apps use Row-Bot's own uv and Python. Container images need Docker Desktop, already installed, and never get access to your folders, ports or network. If what an app would install changes after you agreed, Row-Bot shows it again and waits. - **Open _program_**: apps that work with a program on this computer, such as Blender, check that it is running. Open it, then choose **Check again**. Searching and reading an app's page never install or run anything; nothing installs until you agree and choose **Install**. **Stop** cancels a setup and keeps what was already done. A setup left waiting for more than 30 minutes stops by itself, also keeping what was done. If Row-Bot can't confirm that a change finished, the page shows **Finishing your last change...** with **Retry**; it checks the result and never repeats the change blindly. ## Choose What An App Can Do | Choice | What it means | | --- | --- | | **Read only** | Looks things up. Cannot change anything. | | **Ask before changes** (default) | Looks things up and asks you before every change. | | **Full access** | Makes routine changes without asking. Risky actions still ask. | **Customise** sets each action on its own: **Use without asking**, **Ask first**, **Off**, or **As chosen above**. To change it later, use **Choose** in the app's **Access** section. Some apps overlap with what Row-Bot already does, for example Notion with documents or Slack with channels. Their access step notes it, such as "Row-Bot also has its own Documents tools.", and the choices work as usual. Changes to files and repositories, such as creating a file or a pull request, always ask first. :::info Some actions always ask Deleting, sending, paying, publishing, running code and anything Row-Bot can't identify always ask first, whatever you choose. Full access only covers routine changes such as creating or editing. Apps connected before this version keep asking before routine changes until you choose otherwise. ::: ### In Chats And Workflows An app's access applies wherever Row-Bot uses it, together with the chat's or workflow's **Approvals**. **Auto** lets routine changes run without asking, but actions that always ask still ask, and a workflow waits for you on them; **Block** leaves out anything that would ask. Approval cards name the app and the action, such as "Allow Notion to delete page?"; see [Approvals](/docs/chat/tools-approvals-and-terminal#approvals). ## Change Settings After Setup A connected app's settings stay editable. Its **Settings** section shows what it is set to now: the account, whether a key is saved, each setting (a switch reads **Yes** or **No**), and where it runs. **Change settings** opens **Settings for _app_** with every setting the app has, optional ones too: - A saved key is never shown. Its field stays empty and says **Saved in your system keychain. Leave it blank to keep it.** Type a new key only to replace it. - **Save** keeps your changes, and Row-Bot checks the connection again. If the app now offers actions it didn't have before, Row-Bot asks what they may do first; the rest keep the access you chose. - An app that was on reconnects with the new settings; one that was off stays off until you turn it on. The page then says **Settings saved.** A built-in way's settings are changed in its own settings: choose **Open**, or ** Open its settings**. ## Turn Off Or Remove Both are in the app's **** menu. - **Turn off** stops Row-Bot using the app and ends its connection. Its settings and saved keys are kept, and **Turn on** brings it back. - **Remove...** opens **Remove _app_** and removes the app with its settings and access choices. Its saved sign-in and keys stay in your system keychain unless you switch on **Also delete saved keys and data**, which is offered when it has any. - **Removing a package** removes it and everything it brought, but keeps its saved data and keys: its card then says **Removed**, and **Delete saved data** deletes them. Switch on **Also delete saved keys and data** to delete them straight away. An app that came with a package can be turned off, but is removed with its package. Removing never revokes access at the service; do that in the service's own settings. Shared runtimes such as Node.js and uv, and what Row-Bot downloaded to run an app on this computer, stay installed. A built-in way has neither action; use its own settings instead, such as an account's access switches or **Disconnect**, a channel's **Stop**, or a key tool's switch. ## Add From Link Or File **Add from link or file** adds something that isn't in a catalog. Paste an https link (an app's address, a GitHub repository or a skill page; Row-Bot detects which, and **This is** lets you change it), or choose a .zip or .skill file (up to 20 MB) for skills and packages, or a .mcpb bundle (up to 128 MB). A bundle is checked as soon as you choose it: Row-Bot reads its manifest, checks that it runs on this computer and, if it is signed, that the signature matches its contents. A bundle with a broken signature, or made for another system, is refused. The settings a bundle asks for become its **Add your settings** step. A key pasted as part of a link is never saved with the address: Row-Bot asks for it as a key instead. Nothing is downloaded or run until you agree on the item's page. ## Advanced **Advanced** on the Apps page (`/settings/apps?view=advanced`) holds: - **Catalogs**: see [Update catalogs](#update-catalogs). - **Apps in chats**: **Use apps** (turn off to stop every app at once; each keeps its settings), **Show app views in chat** (interactive views from apps that have them; on by default), whether chats are offered app tools (**Use apps in chats**), and **Runtimes**, the Node.js and uv that Row-Bot sets up for apps that run on this computer. - **Your own connection**: **Add a custom connection** opens the connection editor for a service that isn't in a catalog. An app's ** Advanced settings** opens the raw settings for that one app only. ## Update Catalogs Row-Bot ships a copy of each catalog, so search works offline. **Apps Advanced Catalogs** lists each catalog with its state, such as **Included with Row-Bot**, **Updated** with the time and number of entries, **Couldn't update. The last copy is still used.**, or **Not available yet**. - **Update** refreshes one catalog, and **Update all** every catalog that can be updated. - **Update catalogs automatically** is off by default. Turn it on and choose **Every day**, **Every week** or **Every month**. - **Windows connectors** appears only on Windows builds that have them. **Composio**, a hosted broker, stays off until you turn on **Use Composio** after reading what it means; see [Hosted brokers](/docs/integrations/mcp#hosted-brokers-composio). A failed update keeps the last copy. Behind a proxy, see [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/#apps-and-skills). ## Old Links Settings no longer has Integrations, MCP, Plugins, Accounts or Channels pages. Old links to them open **Apps**, or **Apps Advanced** for catalogs and runtimes, or the item they named: an old account or channel link opens that app, such as **Apps Google** or **Apps Telegram**, and an old Channels link that named no channel opens the **Communication** apps. Skills are on their own page: see [Settings: Skills](/docs/settings/skills). ## Privacy And Safety Searching, browsing and opening an app page stay on this computer. A catalog is contacted only when you choose **Search online catalogs**, **Update**, or automatic updates; updating the Hermes catalog also reads each new package's manifest, never its code. Once you agree to connect, add or update something, Row-Bot reads it from its source, for example to check its listing again or to download what it installs. Requests to an app go where its page says once you use it. Keys, tokens and OAuth client secrets are kept in your system keychain, never in settings files, logs or what the page shows. Row-Bot's sign-in details are published at `https://row-bot.ai/oauth/client-metadata.json`; they contain no secret and name only this computer as where a sign-in returns. Checking that a program is open looks only at this computer. Apps that run on this computer are not sandboxed, so add only apps you trust. ## Control-Level Reference The [generated Settings Controls reference](/docs/reference/generated/settings-controls#apps-controls) lists every searchable setting on this page with its deep link and search keywords. ## Troubleshooting Each status has one fix: the main action on the app's page, also offered in Overview's **Needs you**. [Troubleshooting](/docs/troubleshooting/#apps-and-skills) lists every status, and catalog, proxy, Windows connector and app view problems. - If an app's tools are missing in chat, check that it is **Ready**, that it is checked in that chat's **+ Apps**, that **Use apps** is on and **Apps in chats** offers app tools, and that the chat's agent profile allows it. - A built-in account or channel that won't work: choose **Open** on its app page and use its own **Check**, **Reconnect** or **Start**.

## Settings: Preferences

Route: /docs/settings/preferences

Set the assistant's name and personality, learning new skills, how Row-Bot opens, the overnight Dream Cycle, and this device's appearance.

# Settings: Preferences Preferences are personal choices: how Row-Bot introduces itself, how it opens, and when it tidies memory overnight. **Appearance**, the page after it in the **General** group, sets how Row-Bot looks on this device. ## Where To Find It Open **Settings**, then choose **Preferences** in the **General** group, or search for it with **Find a setting**. ## Identity - **Name** is the assistant's name. - **Personality** sets the assistant's default tone; a preview shows how it sounds. - **Learn new skills** lets Row-Bot write and refine skills from your work. Turn it off to keep the skill library exactly as you set it. ## Opening Row-Bot **Open in** chooses whether Row-Bot opens in its own app window, in your browser, or asks each time. ## Overnight Tidy-Up **Dream Cycle** tidies memory while you are away: it merges duplicates, enriches thin memories and infers missing links. Choose the **Hours** it may run (start and end hour). Its runs appear in Monitor's **History**, and Home Knowledge can run it at any time. ## Appearance **Settings Appearance** applies to this device only, so a phone and a computer can look different: - **Appearance**: **System** (follows your device), **Light** or **Dark**. - **Colour theme**: **Blue**, **Teal**, **Violet** or **Amber**. - **Density**: **Comfortable** or **Compact**. - **Reduce transparency** turns off the glass effect. - **Workspace layout Panel sizes** restores panel sizes without changing conversations or the look. A preview shows the result as you choose. In the command palette, "dark mode", "light mode" and "follow the system appearance" change it in one step. ## What Moved - **Updates** (the update channel and checking for new versions) is its own page in the **System** group. See [Operations, Data, And Recovery](/docs/operations/#update-repair-and-uninstall). - **Import from another assistant** (Hermes Agent or OpenClaw) is on **Settings Data**, with back up and restore. See [Operations, Data, And Recovery](/docs/operations/#back-up). ## What Is Saved Preferences are global local settings. Appearance is saved on each device. Existing conversations keep their own model, profile and approval choices. ## Privacy And Safety These settings stay on your computer. Dream Cycle works on local memory and uses your chosen model when it needs one, which may be a hosted provider. ## Control-Level Reference The [generated Settings Controls reference](/docs/reference/generated/settings-controls#preferences-controls) lists every searchable setting on this page with its deep link, search keywords, and any dependency or security notes. ## Troubleshooting - If the app opens in the wrong place, change **Open in** and restart Row-Bot. - If Dream Cycle never runs, check that it is on and that its hours include times your computer is awake. - If the look differs between devices, that is expected: Appearance is saved per device.

## Extend Row-Bot

Route: /docs/extending/

Choose between built-in tools, Skills, Custom Tools, packages, apps, channels, and accounts, and how Row-Bot sets apps and skills up.

# Extend Row-Bot Start with the narrowest extension type that can solve the task. Every extension adds capabilities; some also add code, dependencies, network access, credentials, or external side effects. For the conceptual differences between tools, Skills, plugins, MCP, channels, and accounts, read [Extensions And Trust Boundaries](/docs/concepts/extensions-and-trust). | Extension | Use It For | Review Boundary | | --- | --- | --- | | Built-in tool | A capability already shipped and maintained with Row-Bot. | Enable only the tools a profile needs; consequential operations still use approval policy. | | Skill | Reusable instructions and workflow knowledge. | Open **What's inside** before adding it; adding turns it on, and its scripts never run when added. | | Custom Tool | A reviewed local command or repo-specific helper made from a folder in Settings Tools or a code folder's Developer panel. | Inspect its source, command classification, dependencies, and workspace scope. | | Plugin (package) | A packaged bundle that can provide tools, skills, apps, configuration, or UI. | Review its page, publisher, **Included** items, and downloads before adding it. | | App | Tools from a hosted service, or from a program that runs on this computer. | Review where requests go and choose **Read only** or **Ask before changes** until you trust it. | | Channel | A messaging adapter for receiving or delivering work. | Verify account, recipients, pairing, tunnel, and delivery defaults before starting. | | Account | Authorisation for GitHub, Google, X, or another service used by tools. | Review requested scopes and disconnect unused accounts. | ## Safe Evaluation Sequence 1. Read the extension's page: what it does, who publishes it, and its source. 2. Check where requests go, what it needs (a sign-in, a key, downloads), and what it includes. Nothing is fetched or run until you agree. 3. Add it only from a source you trust. 4. Choose **Read only** or **Ask before changes** for an app until you trust it. 5. Test with fictional data and a non-consequential task; **Try it** prepares a draft without sending it. 6. Keep the conversation's approval mode at **Ask** until behaviour is familiar. 7. Turn off or remove extensions that are no longer maintained or needed. Third-party dependency telemetry is not Row-Bot telemetry. Review and accept any dependency behaviour before installation, and never allow it to receive Row-Bot prompts, files, memories, secrets, screenshots, tool arguments, or channel content unless that transfer is the explicit feature you chose. Connect apps and packages in [Settings Apps](/docs/settings/apps), where your accounts and channels are apps too, and add skills in [Settings Skills](/docs/settings/skills). Open an item's page, read what will happen, and agree; Row-Bot then does the setup and asks what the app may do. Raw settings for one item stay under its ** Advanced settings**. ## How Apps And Skills Are Set Up This section is for developers working on Row-Bot or building against its local API. Five guides go further: - [Catalog Source Adapters](/docs/extending/source-adapters): add a catalog, and the passive-read rules. - [Contribute To The App Catalog](/docs/extending/app-catalog): app records, verified vendors, icons, featured skills and coverage. - [MCP Bundles (.mcpb)](/docs/extending/mcp-bundles): what Row-Bot reads, checks and runs in a bundle. - [Sign-In And Client Metadata](/docs/extending/sign-in-and-client-metadata): CIMD, dynamic registration and your own OAuth app. - [Hosting MCP Apps Views](/docs/extending/mcp-apps): the sandboxed frame, its bridge and its limits. **Plans.** For each action on an item, the server computes an install plan: an ordered list of typed steps (`consent`, `inputs`, `runtime`, `local_app_check`, `sign_in`, `test`, `access`, `enable`). `POST /api/v1/integrations/plans/review` returns the plan with a consent token bound to the session and the plan's digest. `POST /api/v1/integrations/plans` starts it with that token; the server runs it in the background, and the client polls `GET /api/v1/integrations/plans/{id}`. A plan paused for input resumes with `POST .../plans/{id}/continue` and stops with `POST .../plans/{id}/cancel`, keeping completed steps. A paused plan expires after 30 minutes. When the outcome of a step is uncertain, the plan reports it rather than re-running it. **Intents.** `connect`, `add`, `turn_on`, `fix`, `access`, `settings` (change a connected MCP app's declared inputs: one `inputs` step with every setting, then `test`, `access`, which pauses only when the tools changed, and `enable`, which reconnects only if it was on), `turn_off`, `remove` (with `cleanup` to also delete saved keys and data, bound to the consent) and `update`. **Built-in ways.** `integrations/builtin.py` lists Row-Bot's own accounts, channels and key tools as items (`builtin:account:<id>`, `builtin:channel:<id>`, `builtin:tool:<id>`) with their status read from their owners. They have no plan: their page opens the owner's settings scoped to that item (`?edit=1`). Each keeps its owner's credentials; an account's token is never another app's key. **Endpoints.** All under `/api/v1/integrations/`: `sources` (with `sources/{id}/update` and, for a broker, `sources/{id}/opt-in`), `apps`, `icons` (a batch of logos as data URIs), `items`, `items/search`, `items/resolve`, `items/settle`, `uploads`, `detail`, `plans/review`, `plans`, `plans/{id}`, `plans/{id}/continue`, `plans/{id}/cancel`, `catalog-schedule`, `views` (with `views/apps`) and `workflow-templates` (with `workflow-templates/{id}/use`). `items` reads installed items or the local catalog index (by `scope`); `items/search` with `refresh` is the explicit **Search online catalogs**; `items/resolve` identifies a pasted link without fetching it (an app link with a query string is refused, since keys belong in the keychain); `uploads` stages a picked file and is limited to Row-Bot on this computer; `items/settle` is the **Retry** on an unfinished change: it checks that item's unfinished owner commands again and settles each only when its owner proves how it ended, never re-sending one. The old `/settings/integrations` API routes are removed. **Tool access.** Each MCP tool is classified by effect: - High-impact tools always ask: those with `destructiveHint`, or whose name or description has a verb such as delete, send, post, publish, deploy, merge, push, commit, run, execute, pay, transfer, upload, comment, share, invite, permission, reset or overwrite. A routine verb on a sensitive noun (release, message, email, script, password, role, member, collaborator, token, secret, key, admin, owner, webhook, pull request, user, visibility, membership, file, repository) is high-impact too. A tool whose change shows only in its description is unknown and always asks. - Routine changes (create, add, update, edit, write, set, rename, move and similar; tag, label, archive, link or copy only as the name's leading verb) ask unless the tool is listed in the server's `tools.run_without_asking`, which **Full access** or a per-tool **Use without asking** sets. - Unknown effects always ask. - Annotations only make a tool stricter; `readOnlyHint` is the one exception and never outweighs a change verb in the name. Policies saved before `run_without_asking` existed have no entries in it, so their routine changes keep asking. A server that overlaps a native capability gets `PlanAccess.note` ("Row-Bot also has its own ... tools."); presets apply as usual. See [MCP](/docs/integrations/mcp) for the user-facing description. **Search.** The local index (`integrations/index.py`) ranks vendor-verified and featured entries first, never lets a Registry namespace word (`io`, `github`, `com`) match unless the query is the namespace, and hides low-quality listings (template titles, staging copies, empty descriptions, duplicate title and description) behind `all=true`, reporting how many as `hidden`. `sources.rank` merges one deployment listed twice and groups one card per app; `IntegrationAbout.ways` lists an app's other ways to connect. **Declared inputs.** What a connection needs from the person is declared once, whatever the source (a Registry header, URL variable, environment variable or argument; a plugin's `mcp.json` `${VAR}`; a Hermes recipe's keys; a bundle's `user_config`). The saved configuration keeps the template (`"Authorization": "Bearer {token}"`, `https://{tenant}.example.com/mcp`, `"--region", "{region}"`) with the declarations in `inputs` (`key`, `label`, `description`, `secret`, `required`, `target`, `name`, `default`, `choices`, `help_url`, `format`, `flag`). Plain values go to `input_values`; secrets go to one keychain credential with `input` bindings. Values are filled in only at connection time (`integrations/inputs.resolve`). A URL variable may fill a path segment, a query value or a subdomain label under a fixed registrable domain, never the host; variables that change what runs (`PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS`, `LD_PRELOAD` and similar) are never declared. A bare token typed for an `Authorization` header is sent as `Bearer`. **Sign-in.** The `test` step detects a sign-in (a 401 with protected-resource and authorization-server metadata) and turns `sign_in` on. Row-Bot then uses the person's own client, its Client ID Metadata Document, dynamic client registration, or a pause for the person's own client ID and secret. A refresh that fails marks the app **Sign in needed**. See [Sign-In And Client Metadata](/docs/extending/sign-in-and-client-metadata). **Runtimes and locks.** A local server's package is resolved into a lock before it installs: `npm` (the registry's shrinkwrap, a managed `npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts`, or a self-contained package's own metadata), `pypi` (managed uv: `uv pip compile --generate-hashes --only-binary :all:`), `oci` (`docker pull`, then the image's repository digest) or `mcpb`. Each lock lists every item with its version and integrity and has its own digest. The `runtime` step pauses `digest_changed` with that review, and continues only with `review_digest` equal to it; a plan whose saved recipe changed under it fails `plan_changed`. Installs go into a private folder per server (npm tarballs checked against their `sha512`, wheels installed with `--require-hashes --no-deps`), install scripts never run, and the launch is the reviewed one. Docker runs `run -i --rm --pull=never` on the locked digest, with no mounts, published ports, privileges or network changes. Nothing runs before consent. **MCP bundles.** `mcp_client/bundles.py` reads and checks a `.mcpb` without running it; a bundle is locked by its file's digest, and `{bundle}` in its launch is its extracted folder. See [MCP Bundles (.mcpb)](/docs/extending/mcp-bundles). **Local apps.** An app in `apps.json` may declare `local_check` (`{"port": 9876}` or a process name). The `local_app_check` step connects only to `127.0.0.1` on that port or looks for that exact process, and pauses with **Check again** until it is there. **Hermes catalog.** Updating the Hermes source also reads each new pin's `plugin.json` (manifest only, never code); a package without an Agent Plugins manifest is native to Hermes and listed as unavailable. Hermes MCP recipes are read at their pin after consent, shown for review (`digest_changed`) and then set up with the steps above. **Live checks.** `tests/e2e/test_github_live.py` (`e2e`, `live_provider`) checks a GitHub connection made in the UI against an isolated data folder, without ever handling its token: run it with `ROW_BOT_TEST_MODE=0`, `ROW_BOT_GITHUB_LIVE_DATA` set to that folder (the suite gives every test its own folder, so the live one is named separately) and `ROW_BOT_GITHUB_LIVE=connected`, then `removed` after removing the app. Mark a recipe `tested_with_row_bot` only after its live check passes.

## Accounts And Authorisation

Route: /docs/integrations/accounts

Connect your GitHub, Google and X accounts as apps, set Google up with your own OAuth client, and keep scopes, tokens and data flow understandable.

# Accounts And Authorisation Accounts let selected tools act through services such as GitHub, Google, or X. A model provider account supplies models; an integration account supplies service access. They are configured separately. Each account is an app in **Settings Apps**: **GitHub**, **Google** and **X**. On the app's page the account is a **Built in** way to connect, and it is set up in its own settings, which show only that account. ## Connect Safely 1. Open **Settings Apps** and choose the app, or type "connect google", "connect github" or "connect x" in the command palette. 2. On the app's page, choose **Set up** (or **Open** once it is set up). The account's own settings open with a numbered setup guide; each step links to the page it needs, and finished steps are ticked. 3. Prefer the supported OAuth or local CLI flow rather than pasting broad tokens. 4. Verify the service, account, and scopes in the external authorisation page. 5. Back in Row-Bot, **Check** confirms the account works. 6. Test a read-only action before approving writes, posts, email, calendar, or repository changes. Each account shows its state (**Connected**, **Not checked yet**, **Needs reconnecting** or **Not connected**) with **Check**, **Reconnect** when a sign-in expired, and **Disconnect**. Disconnecting asks first and removes the sign-in from this computer; it doesn't revoke access at the service, which you can do in the service's own settings. ## GitHub 1. Sign in with the GitHub CLI on this computer (**Sign in with the GitHub CLI**, offered when the CLI is installed), or **Create a token**: a fine-grained token for the repositories Row-Bot should use. 2. If you made a token, paste it under **GitHub token**. It stays in your keychain. 3. **Check GitHub** confirms Row-Bot can reach GitHub. Public repositories work without an account; **Use public access only** says so. GitHub's page also lists GitHub's hosted server and its server on this computer as other ways to connect. Each keeps its own token: the GitHub account's token is never used for a GitHub server connection, or the other way round. ## Google Row-Bot has no Google sign-in of its own. You create a Desktop app OAuth client in your own Google Cloud project, give Row-Bot its file, and sign in with it. The account connects **Gmail** and **Google Calendar**. The guide, **How to set up Google**, links straight to each Google page: 1. **Create a project**: sign in to Google Cloud and create a project for Row-Bot. Any name works. 2. **Turn on both APIs**: one link turns on the Gmail and Google Calendar APIs for that project. 3. **Open Branding**: give your sign-in a name, such as "My Row-Bot", and your email address. 4. **Open Audience**: choose **External**, then add your own Google address as a test user. 5. **Create the client**: create a client of type **Desktop app** and download its file straight away, because Google shows its secret only then. In Row-Bot, choose that file with **Choose file...** under **Google sign-in file**; any file name works. 6. **Sign in with Google**, then finish signing in in your browser. **Gmail access** and **Calendar access** choose what Row-Bot may do: it can search, read and draft email, but sending always asks first; it can see and add events, but moving or deleting asks first. Google's own hosted Workspace servers are a developer preview open only to testers, so the Google account with your own client is the recommended way to connect Google. ### Google Sign-Ins In Testing Last 7 Days Google limits apps whose publishing status is **Testing**, as a new app made with the steps above is: - A sign-in lasts 7 days from when you agree to it; after that Google stops Row-Bot renewing it. - At most 100 test users can sign in. When the sign-in expires, Row-Bot shows it: **Apps Google** says **Sign in needed** with **Sign in again**, the account's settings say **Needs reconnecting** with **Reconnect**, and Overview's **Needs you** lists **Sign in to Google**. Signing in again gives you another 7 days. To stop it, publish your app: in Google Cloud, open **Audience** and choose **Publish app**, so its status is **In production**, then sign in again. Because Gmail and Calendar access are sensitive or restricted Google scopes and your app isn't verified by Google, Google then shows its unverified-app warning when you sign in; continuing is fine for an app you made for yourself. An unverified app can be used by at most 100 people, and you don't need Google's verification for your own use. ## X 1. In the X developer portal (**Open the developer portal**), create a project and an app, with OAuth 2.0 read and write turned on. 2. Copy the callback address the guide shows into the app's sign-in settings. 3. Paste the app's client ID and secret. 4. **Connect X**, then finish signing in in your browser. **X access** chooses what Row-Bot may do. Posting and deleting ask first. ## Tokens And Scopes Secrets use the configured operating-system secret store when available. Settings show status, not the secret value. A service may still retain its own authorisation grant until you revoke it there. Use the narrowest scopes that support the feature and disconnect access you no longer use. ## When A Sign-In Expires Overview's **Needs you** shows the app, such as **Sign in to Google**, with a button that opens the account's own settings at its fix. Monitor offers **Reconnect Google** or **Reconnect X**, which starts the sign-in again on the computer Row-Bot runs on. ## Troubleshooting - Confirm the system browser returned to the same Row-Bot instance that started the flow. - For GitHub CLI, refresh CLI authorisation after signing in or changing accounts. - If Row-Bot says the Google file isn't a valid Google OAuth client file, create a client of type **Desktop app** and download its file again. - If Google asks you to sign in again every week, your Google app is still in Testing; publish it in **Audience** (see [Google Sign-Ins In Testing Last 7 Days](#google-sign-ins-in-testing-last-7-days)). - If a callback fails, repeat the supported flow instead of copying browser storage. - If an action is denied after connection, review both the service scopes and the Row-Bot approval policy.

## Channels

Route: /docs/integrations/channels

Connect Row-Bot to messaging channels as apps: setup steps, pairing, public addresses, delivery, and safe external behavior.

# Channels Channels connect Row-Bot to external messaging platforms: Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, and SMS through Twilio. Use channels when you want to message Row-Bot outside the desktop app or send workflow results somewhere specific. Each channel is an app in **Settings Apps**, under the **Communication** category: **Telegram**, **WhatsApp**, **Discord**, **Slack** and **Text messages** (SMS). On the app's page the channel is a **Built in** way to connect. Slack's page also lists Slack's own hosted server, which lets Row-Bot work in your Slack workspace rather than talk to you through it. A package can bring a channel too; it is listed with its package. ## Setup Workflow 1. Open **Settings Apps** and choose the channel's app, or type "connect telegram" (or the channel you want) in the command palette. 2. Choose **Set up** (or **Open** once it is set up). The channel's own settings open, showing only that channel. 3. Follow **Connect _channel_**. Each step says what to do where, links to the platform's page (such as **Open @BotFather** for Telegram), and has its field in place: paste a value and choose **Save** for it. 4. Choose **Start _channel_**. A channel that needs a public address, such as SMS, opens your tunnel by itself; its setup is the public link in **Settings Devices & remote access**. WhatsApp's first start installs its bridge, then shows a code to scan with your phone. 5. Pair or approve your account before trusting private messages: **Get pairing code for _channel_**, then send the code to the bot from the account you want to approve. 6. **Send a test message to me** to check it works with a low-risk message. ## Controls - **Save** and **Clear** beside each field store or remove that value. Saved values are never shown again. - **Start _channel_** begins the channel; it starts again with Row-Bot until you stop it. **Stop _channel_** shuts it down. - **Reachable at** shows the public address a channel uses, with **Copy**. - **Get pairing code for _channel_** shows a code that approves the account that sends it; it expires after one hour. Some channels approve people their own way and say so. - **Paired accounts** lists who is approved, with **Revoke** for each. - **Reset session** (WhatsApp) unlinks your phone and shows a new code to scan. - **More settings** holds the channel's other fields. - **`/reasoning`** shows or changes the reasoning choice for that channel conversation's active model. Run it without an argument to see the exact valid choices. ## Safety Messages sent through a channel leave the local app. Do not enable a channel until you understand who can message it, what Row-Bot can send back, and whether workflows may deliver results there. When work starts from a channel and a child agent asks for approval, Row-Bot sends the approval back to that parent channel conversation when the channel supports approval messages. The same approval stays visible in the parent conversation, the sidebar's attention indicator and Overview's **Needs you**, and an answer in any of them resolves it everywhere. ## Troubleshooting - If Telegram encounters one transient network failure during initialization, Row-Bot cleans up the partial runtime and retries once. Persistent network failures remain stopped with an actionable diagnostic; invalid bot tokens are not retried. - If Telegram starts but its command menu cannot be registered, polling remains available and the menu failure is logged as non-fatal. - If a channel cannot start, check its fields and the public link. Automatic tunnel startup runs outside the UI event loop, so a slow tunnel helper should report status without freezing app startup. - If a channel stopped, Monitor offers **Restart _channel_** for it. - If inbound messages fail, verify webhook URLs and platform permissions. - If the wrong person has access, revoke them from **Paired accounts**.

## Skills

Route: /docs/skills/

Find, add, use, turn off, remove, create and troubleshoot Row-Bot skills, and how Row-Bot picks them automatically.

# Skills Skills are instruction packs that teach Row-Bot how to approach a category of work. **Settings Skills** is where you find skills, add them, try them, and create or edit your own (the command palette's **Add a skill** goes there). Skills you have added can also be discovered and loaded progressively when a task clearly matches their purpose. See [Settings: Skills](/docs/settings/skills) for the page itself. ## UI Walkthrough - **Search** finds skills in the library on this computer; **Search online catalogs** asks catalogs such as ClawHub. - **Your skills** lists the skills you have added, built-in and your own. - **A skill's page** shows its slash command (**Use it in chat with /_name_**), whether chats use it and which agent profiles include it, and **What's inside**: its files and scripts. - **Add** adds the skill and turns it on. Scripts inside it never run when it is added. - **Try it** opens a new chat with a draft that uses the skill; nothing is sent until you send it. - ** Turn off** stops chats using it, and ** Remove...** deletes a skill you added or created. - ** Advanced settings** opens the skill editor, where you edit and pin the skill and review proposed changes. ## Creating A Skill 1. Choose **Create a skill** in Settings Skills. 2. Decide what task the skill should help with. 3. Write concise instructions, examples, and boundaries, including when the skill should and should not be used. 4. Save it. 5. Test it with **Try it** or a small prompt. 6. Revise if Row-Bot overuses or misunderstands it. ## What Skills Change Skills shape Row-Bot's behavior; they do not automatically grant credentials or bypass approvals. A skill can make Row-Bot more consistent for a task, but tools still need to be enabled and approved where appropriate. ## Automatic Selection When progressive discovery is available, Row-Bot can search enabled skills and load a relevant one for the current task. A successful automatic load appears once as **Using _skill_** and adds an active skill chip. - Automatically selected skills are stored per parent task or child Agent, not per shared Agent Profile. - Reopening a task restores its selected skills. - Parent tasks and sibling children do not share automatic activation state. - Up to five automatically selected skills are retained per task; pinned skills remain separate. - Loading an already active skill does not show a second **Using _skill_** notice. Automatic selection changes instructions only. It cannot add a denied tool, alter credentials, bypass approvals, expand a workspace, or change an Agent Profile. Read [Progressive Tools And Skills](/docs/guides/progressive-tools-and-skills) for the complete tool and skill flow. ## Troubleshooting - If a skill is not used, make your prompt match its purpose, confirm it is in **Your skills**, or call it with its slash command. The command on its own turns the skill on for the chat; inside a longer message it focuses just that turn on the skill. See [Mention an app or a skill](/docs/chat/#mention-an-app-or-a-skill). - If a skill is too aggressive, rewrite it with clearer boundaries or remove it. - If a skill from a catalog is unfamiliar, open **What's inside** before adding it.

## Packages (Plugins)

Route: /docs/integrations/plugins

Add, turn off, and remove packages of apps and skills in Settings Apps.

# Packages (Plugins) A package (plugin) bundles several things, such as apps, skills and settings, under one name. Packages are managed in [Settings Apps](/docs/settings/apps) like any other app. ## Add A Package Find it in **Settings Apps**, or use **Add from link or file** with a GitHub repository or a .zip file. Package rows from the Hermes catalog say **Checked when you add**: Row-Bot checks what the package contains when you add it, not while you browse. Nothing is downloaded or run until you agree on its page. The package page's **Included** section lists what it brings. Each of those items says **Installed as part of _package_** and is managed through the package. Finish any app inside it that still needs a sign-in or a key from its own page. ## Turn Off And Remove - **Turn off** stops the package and everything it brought. Settings and keys are kept. - **Remove...** removes the package and everything it brought. Its saved keys and data are kept unless you choose **Also delete saved keys and data**; while they are kept, its card says **Removed** and **Delete saved data** deletes them. - **Check for updates**, for a package from GitHub, downloads its newest version and checks it before anything changes. Shared runtimes such as Node.js and uv stay installed. ## Safety A package does not skip approvals or agent profile limits; its apps follow the access you choose for them. Code a package runs on this computer is not sandboxed, so add packages only from publishers you trust. Hooks and entry points written for other assistants are not run. See [Extend Row-Bot](/docs/extending/) for how packages compare with skills, apps and Custom Tools.

## Hosted And Local Apps (MCP)

Route: /docs/integrations/mcp

How apps that are hosted or run on this computer connect, which of their actions ask first, Windows connectors, the Composio broker, and turning apps off or removing them.

# Hosted And Local Apps (MCP) Most apps in [Settings Apps](/docs/settings/apps) connect in one of two ways: **Hosted**, where the service runs the connection, or **Runs on this computer**, where Row-Bot starts a small program for it. Both use the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for offering tools to assistants; you never need to know that to use them. ## Connect An App - **From a catalog**: search **Settings Apps**, open the app and choose **Connect** or **Add**. Row-Bot shows what will happen, then sets up anything the app needs to run (Node.js or uv, and the app's own package) in its own folder, asks for any key or setting, checks the connection (and signs you in if the service asks), and asks what the app can do. - **From a link or file**: **Add from link or file** accepts an app's https address, a GitHub repository, or a `.mcpb` bundle. - **By its settings**: **Apps Advanced Add a custom connection** opens the connection editor for an app that isn't in a catalog. Use separate connections with their own names for separate accounts, such as Work and Personal. Keys are kept in your system keychain. **Apps Advanced Apps in chats** controls whether chats are offered app tools, and shows the shared Node.js and uv runtimes. ## Which Actions Ask First When you choose what an app can do, Row-Bot groups its actions by effect: - **Looks things up**: actions that only read. Read only, Ask before changes and Full access all let these run. - **Makes changes**: routine changes such as create, add, update, edit, write, set, rename or move. They ask first unless you chose **Full access** or set the action to **Use without asking**. - **Always asks first**: high-impact actions. An action is high-impact when the app marks it destructive, or when its name or description says it does something such as delete, send, post, publish, deploy, merge, push, commit, run, execute, pay, transfer, upload, comment, share, invite or change permissions. A routine change to something that reaches people, publishes or grants access is high-impact too, for example creating a release or a pull request, adding a collaborator or setting a password. These ask in every choice and can't be set to run without asking. An action whose effect Row-Bot can't determine always asks. An app's own hints can only make an action stricter; the one exception is a read-only hint, and it never outweighs a name that says the action makes a change. Without that hint, an action whose name doesn't say it makes a change but whose description does always asks. Connections set up before this version keep asking before routine changes until you choose otherwise. High-impact actions and actions whose effect Row-Bot can't determine ask even when a chat or workflow uses **Auto** approvals: Auto lets routine actions run, never these. Approval mode, agent profiles and the model's tool support still apply on top of this. Turning an action off in Row-Bot does not revoke access at the service; use the service's own account controls for that. ## Interactive Views Some apps can show their results as an interactive view, such as a chart, a form or a board, under the step in chat. A view runs in its own sandbox and goes through the same access and approvals as any other call. See [App views](/docs/chat/#app-views); developers can read [Hosting MCP Apps Views](/docs/extending/mcp-apps). ## Windows Connectors On Windows Insider builds with Windows' On-device Agent Registry (build 26220.7344 or later, with **Settings System AI components Experimental agentic features** on), **Apps Advanced Catalogs** lists **Windows connectors**: connectors that Windows and your installed apps provide. Choose **Update** to list them; Row-Bot asks Windows only then. Connecting one is the usual setup, and Windows also asks you to allow it the first time Row-Bot uses it. Row-Bot never adds, removes or configures Windows connectors. On other computers and older builds the catalog isn't shown. ## Hosted Brokers (Composio) A broker is a separate hosted service that connects many apps through one account. **Composio** is off until you turn it on in **Apps Advanced Catalogs** with **Use Composio**, which first explains what it means: a separate Composio account, and the requests and results for apps you use through it pass through Composio, which keeps them for up to a year by default under its own terms. Links to Composio's terms, privacy policy and data processing agreement are shown there, and nothing changes until you choose **Turn on Composio**. While it's on, searching for an app also finds Composio, and an app's page offers a way such as **Notion via Composio** after the app's own ways to connect. Connecting signs you in to Composio (or takes a consumer key, kept in your keychain); you then connect each app in your Composio account. Composio's remote code tools start off, and its tools that act for other apps ask every time. Turning the switch off stops Row-Bot offering Composio; a Composio connection you already made stays until you turn it off or remove it on its page. Pipedream isn't available. ## Turn Off And Remove **Turn off** stops the connection and keeps its settings and keys. **Remove...** removes the connection and its settings; its saved sign-in and keys stay in your keychain unless you choose **Also delete saved keys and data**. Shared runtimes stay installed. See [Turn off or remove](/docs/settings/apps#turn-off-or-remove). ## Developers How setup runs on the server, the HTTP API and the tool classification are summarised in [Extend Row-Bot](/docs/extending/#how-apps-and-skills-are-set-up), with guides to catalog sources, the app catalog, bundles, sign-in and views.

## Voice And Buddy

Route: /docs/voice-and-buddy/

Configure Dictate, Talk, local voice, realtime voice, read-aloud, devices, and Buddy.

# Voice And Buddy Voice and Buddy make Row-Bot feel less like a text box and more like a desktop companion. Voice handles speech input and optional spoken output. Buddy reflects app state and, in the native Windows and macOS apps, can be dragged from the sidebar into a compact always-on-top desktop overlay. ## Voice Modes - **Dictate** turns speech into composer text so you can review it before sending. - **Talk** submits spoken input more directly for conversation. - **Read-aloud** speaks assistant responses when enabled. - **Local voice** uses Whisper by default, or the optional SenseVoice Small engine after you install it explicitly. - **Realtime voice** uses a compatible provider for lower-latency spoken conversation. ## Choosing A Mode Use Dictate when accuracy and review matter. Use Talk when you want a faster hands-light conversation. Use local voice when privacy and offline-style behavior matter. Whisper remains the default local transcription engine. SenseVoice is an optional alternative on Windows, Linux, and Apple Silicon macOS; Intel macOS continues to use Whisper. Use realtime voice when latency matters and you accept internet access, provider requirements, and provider cost. ## Optional SenseVoice Setup Open Settings -> Voice, find **SenseVoice** under **Voice models**, and choose **Install SenseVoice Small**. Then choose it as the Talk or Dictation model under **Speech models**. Installation is an explicit approximately 940 MB download from ModelScope. Row-Bot verifies the contained snapshot before saving it under the active data directory, and normal transcription then uses that local snapshot with update checks disabled. Startup, readiness checks, and ordinary transcription never download or repair the model automatically. ## Devices And Diagnostics Select the microphone and output device in Settings -> Voice. Run diagnostics when audio is silent, delayed, or routed to the wrong device. ## Buddy Controls - **Show Buddy** controls companion visibility. - **Drag to tear off** moves Buddy itself from its sidebar dock into the native desktop overlay. Releasing over the dock cancels the drag. - The overlay follows the selected conversation, whether it is a chat, a design or a code folder, and shares its saved draft, current response, tools, and approval mode. - Enter sends and Shift+Enter adds a line. **Stop** stops the selected thread's active response. - **Simple approvals** can be approved or denied in Buddy. **Complex approvals** open the full thread for review. - **Open full thread**, **Collapse/Expand**, **Dock Buddy**, and **Hide Buddy** are in the overlay menu. - Tear-off is session-scoped; restarting Row-Bot returns placement to the normal sidebar dock. Browser/server mode does not create a native overlay. - **Personality** changes the tone of Buddy cues, and **Bubbles** changes how status appears. - **Look** chooses a bundled or custom appearance; **New look...** makes one with your image model. - **Motion** chooses how lively Buddy is: **Calm**, **Normal** or **Lively**. See [Settings: Buddy](/docs/settings/buddy) for the complete drag, messaging, approval, tray-recovery, and troubleshooting walkthrough. ## Talk To Buddy The desktop overlay accepts typed messages for the thread named in its header. It does not contain a separate microphone control: Talk and Dictate remain in the full Row-Bot thread, where device state, transcription, and provider disclosure are visible. Use **Open full thread**, start Talk or Dictate there, and Buddy will continue reflecting that selected conversation. Use Dictate when you want to review speech as text before sending. Use Talk when you want the configured voice path to submit conversation turns. Undocking Buddy does not change which voice provider is used, create a new voice session, or bypass tool approvals. ## Privacy And Safety Voice input can become chat text. Realtime voice and provider-backed speech may send audio or transcript data to the selected provider. Installing SenseVoice contacts ModelScope for the requested model and standard SDK metadata, but Row-Bot does not send audio, prompts, or usage data; inference stays local after installation. Buddy preferences and assets are local, but custom generation may call a configured media provider. ## Troubleshooting - If Dictate records nothing, check microphone selection and permissions. - If Talk sends too quickly, use Dictate instead. - If SenseVoice reports missing packages, install the `voice` extra for a source checkout or repair the packaged app. If its snapshot is missing or incomplete, reinstall it from Voice settings. - If SenseVoice is unavailable on Intel macOS, select local Whisper instead. - If realtime voice is unavailable, check Providers and Voice Models. - If Buddy does not appear, enable **Show Buddy** or use the tray's **Show Buddy** action when it is torn off. - If Buddy will not undock, use the native Windows or macOS app and start the drag on Buddy itself. Remote browsers and browser/server mode keep it docked.

## Catalog Source Adapters

Route: /docs/extending/source-adapters

For developers: the source adapter interface in src/row_bot/integrations/sources.py, how a new catalog source is added as one adapter plus data, and the passive-read rules every source follows.

# Catalog Source Adapters This page is for developers adding a catalog to **Settings Apps** or **Settings Skills**. Every catalog, from the shipped MCP Registry mirror to ClawHub, is one adapter in `src/row_bot/integrations/sources.py`. The server decides what each adapter may do and serves the list; the client never hard-codes sources. ## The Adapter Interface An adapter subclasses `Source`: | Member | Meaning | | --- | --- | | `id` | Stable id, `[a-z0-9_]{1,40}`, such as `official` or `clawhub`. | | `kind` | What it lists: `skill`, `mcp`, `plugin` or `builtin`. Served as `kinds`. | | `label`, `message` | The name and one plain sentence shown under **Apps Advanced Catalogs**. | | `access` | `local` (shipped data), `snapshot` (a shipped copy that updates), `public` (a live catalog) or `unavailable`. | | `eligibility` | `eligible`, `explicit_only`, `auth_required`, `contract_unresolved` or `unsupported`. Decided on the server; a source that isn't eligible or `explicit_only` only reports its status. | | `network` | `none` (never contacts anything) or `explicit` (contacts its catalog only for an explicit online search or an update). | | `search(Search) -> Found` | Returns rows for `search.query`. Must honour `search.refresh` (true only for **Search online catalogs**), `search.cancelled` and `search.validate`. | | `lookup(reference)` | Resolves one entry from local data only, for its page and its install plan. | | `update(cancelled)` | Only for `network = "explicit"`: refreshes the source's local copy and returns a small summary, or raises. A failed update keeps what the source had. | | `listed()` | False hides the source on this computer, as Windows connectors do where Windows doesn't have them. | | `view()`, `status(**fields)` | The served description and a per-search status (`cached`, `stale`, `pending`, `empty`, `unavailable`...). Rarely overridden. | `Search` carries `owner_id`, `query`, `refresh`, `cancelled`, `validate` and `everything` (the **Show all results** request). Build rows with `_available(...)`, which fills the letter-avatar icon and plain-text description, and add them with `found.add(row, reference)`. The `reference` is what the install plan reads later, so it must be one `plans.compute` understands. Filter with `matches(query, *texts)`, which needs every query word. ## Adding A Source 1. Write one `Source` subclass and add an instance to `SOURCES` at the end of `sources.py`. Its position is its ranking precedence among equal rows. 2. Put its data beside it: shipped package data under `src/row_bot/integrations/`, or a cache that only `update` writes. 3. To let its entries open by id (their page and their plan), add a branch to `catalog_entry()`, which resolves ids from local data only. 4. If it has an `update`, `catalogs.updatable()` picks it up: it appears with **Update** in **Apps Advanced Catalogs** and in the optional schedule. 5. Record the public contract you checked (terms, authentication, rate limits) in `docs/INTEGRATION_SOURCES.md`. 6. Add deterministic tests with a faked catalog under `tests/subsystem/integrations/`. `GET /api/v1/integrations/sources` serves every listed source with its catalog state; `POST /api/v1/integrations/sources/{id}/update` starts an update in the background. ## Passive Reads - **Searching, browsing and opening a page are passive.** They read shipped data, the local index and saved results, and nothing else. They launch no program, install nothing and send nothing. - **Only two things contact a catalog:** an explicit **Search online catalogs** (`POST /api/v1/integrations/items/search` with `refresh`), and an update, chosen by the person or by the schedule they turned on. Each search runs a source under an 8-second deadline. - **Updates fetch through `integrations/safe.py`**: https only, reviewed hosts or public addresses, per-hop redirect checks, size and time caps. Registry icons are fetched only during an update and re-encoded locally; rendering never fetches. - **A catalog listing grants nothing.** Eligibility is decided on the server, and nothing runs before the person agrees to an install plan. The global network guard in `tests/conftest.py` fails any deterministic test that connects off the computer. `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_apps_and_sources.py`, `test_catalog_updates.py` and `tests/subsystem/client_protocol/test_integration_discovery.py` check that passive reads never fetch, that unavailable sources never run, and which sources can update. ## Ranking Ranking lives in `sources.py`, and the local Registry index (`integrations/index.py`) applies the same key in SQL. `order()` puts featured and vendor-verified entries first, then an exact name, a strong text match, featured order, a complete setup, freshness (90 days, a year), the source's popularity and its precedence. `rank()` merges rows that share a source-neutral identity, keeping every source as an attribution, and shows one card per app; `way_order()` orders an app's ways to connect, reviewed and built-in ways first.

## Contribute To The App Catalog

Route: /docs/extending/app-catalog

For developers: the apps.json record format, verified-vendor rules, bundled icons and their licences, the featured skills and broker lists, and how to check catalog coverage.

# Contribute To The App Catalog This page is for developers adding or correcting an app, a featured skill or a logo. The app catalog is package data in `src/row_bot/integrations/`; it is validated when Row-Bot loads it, so a bad record fails loudly instead of showing wrong information. ## App Records (`apps.json`) `apps.json` has `"schema_version": 2` and one record per line under `apps`. Each record is one service people recognise, and catalog entries attach to it only through the references it lists. A record with an unknown field is refused. | Field | Meaning and rules | | --- | --- | | `id` | Lowercase `[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,63}`, unique. Also the page address, `/settings/apps/<id>`. | | `name`, `publisher`, `summary` | The display name, who makes the service, and one plain sentence about what it does. | | `category` | One of `productivity`, `developer`, `data`, `design`, `communication`, `finance` or `local_tools`. | | `synonyms`, `jobs` | Words and tasks people search for, such as "wiki" or "send an email". Search matches them. | | `example_prompts` | Things to ask, shown on the app's page. At least two for an app that has a connection of its own. | | `refs` | The reviewed references that attach catalog entries: `curated:`, `registry:` (an exact server or a namespace), `endpoint:` (a host), `npm:`, `pypi:`, `oci:`, `repo:`, `hermes:`, `bundled:`, and Row-Bot's own `account:`, `channel:` and `tool:` ways. A reference may belong to one app only. | | `vendor` | `domains` and `github_orgs` the vendor controls; the verified badge is granted from these. | | `variants` | The app's ways to connect in its preferred order: `hosted_mcp`, `local_mcp`, `package`, `account`, `channel`, `api_key_tool`, `broker`. | | `auth` | `oauth`, `api_key`, `none`, `account`, `mixed` or empty. | | `docs_url`, `key_url` | https links: the vendor's documentation and where to get a key. | | `icon` | `si:<slug>` for a bundled mark, or empty for a letter avatar. | | `featured_rank` | Optional. Featured apps are ranked 1 to N with no gaps or repeats. | | `local_app`, `local_check` | For an app that works with a program on this computer: its name, and `{"port": 9876}` (a loopback port from 1024 to 65535) or `{"process": "blender"}`. The check looks only at this computer. | | `facts` | `checked` (the date you checked) and `sources`: the vendor pages that support the record. | Unmatched catalog entries stay browsable as **Community**. Never attach an entry by its name alone. ## The Verified Badge **by _Vendor_** with a check is granted by rule, never by a name or a description: - a Registry record is the vendor's when its namespace is a vendor domain reversed (`com.notion` for `notion.com`) or `io.github.<vendor org>`. The Registry checks namespace ownership, so Registry records are judged by namespace alone; - a reviewed recipe or your own connection is the vendor's when its endpoint is under a vendor domain, or is an `endpoint:` the vendor's documentation names exactly. Shared hosting domains, where anyone can have a subdomain (`github.io`, `vercel.app`, `netlify.app`, `pages.dev`, `amazonaws.com`, `supabase.co` and others in `apps.SHARED_HOSTING`), are never vendor domains: the catalog refuses to load with one. Reviewed setup recipes, the **Vendor recommendations** catalog, live in `src/row_bot/mcp_client/recommended_servers.json`. Set a recipe's `tested_with_row_bot` only after its live check passes. ## Icons (`icons.json`) Logos are Simple Icons marks, bundled only for the apps that name them. Each mark in `icons.json` records its `title`, `hex` colour, SVG `path`, `license` (CC0-1.0 for most marks; others record their own), `source` and, where the brand has them, `guidelines`. Rebuild the file from an extracted `simple-icons` package after changing `icon` fields: ```powershell uv run python scripts/build_app_icons.py path/to/simple-icons/package ``` An app without a mark gets a letter avatar drawn locally. Registry icons are fetched only during a catalog update, as raster images from the publisher's own domain, re-encoded locally; remote SVG is never accepted, and drawing a card never fetches anything. ## Featured Skills (`skills.json`) `skills.json` lists references, not copies: each skill is read from its repository at the pinned commit when someone adds it. A record has `id`, `name`, `publisher`, `summary`, `category`, `synonyms`, `jobs`, `repo` (`github.com/<owner>/<repo>`), `path`, `commit` (the full 40-character hash), `license`, `license_url`, `featured_rank`, `checked` and, optionally, `app` (an `apps.json` id). Check the licence at that commit. The library takes permissive and weak-copyleft open-source licences (MIT, Apache-2.0, MPL-2.0 so far); proprietary, unlicensed and share-alike skills stay out. ## Broker Names (`broker_apps.json`) Composio's own catalog can't be listed without an account, so `broker_apps.json` is Row-Bot's own list of well-known app names, each 1 to 80 characters. While Composio is turned on, a search naming one of them shows Composio, and that app's page offers "_App_ via Composio". It is a list of names to search by, not a claim that Composio supports each one. ## Check Coverage `scripts/integration_coverage.py` computes an install plan for every local catalog entry (the reviewed recipes, the whole shipped Registry mirror, featured skills and examples) in a throwaway data folder. It fetches nothing and reads no user data. ```powershell uv run python scripts/integration_coverage.py --output .tmp/integration-coverage ``` It writes `coverage.json` (each entry with "complete" or the exact blocker) and `coverage.md` (counts per source, every blocker, and featured apps without a complete plan). `--hermes` adds a saved Hermes catalog. Run it before and after a catalog change and explain any featured app that stops connecting. ## Tests `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_app_catalog.py`, `test_icons.py`, `test_skill_catalog.py`, `test_brokers.py` and `test_apps_and_sources.py` check the featured ranks, categories, prompts, sources, icon licences, badge rules and attachment. Run them with `uv run python -m pytest tests/subsystem/integrations`.

## MCP Bundles (.mcpb)

Route: /docs/extending/mcp-bundles

For developers: how Row-Bot imports .mcpb bundles, which manifest fields it reads, how user_config becomes setup inputs, platform and runtime checks, signatures, and Registry bundles downloaded only after consent and a checksum match.

# MCP Bundles (.mcpb) This page is for developers who publish an MCP server as an `.mcpb` bundle (formerly `.dxt`) and want it to work in Row-Bot. People add a bundle with **Settings Apps Add from link or file**, or connect a Registry record that points to one. The reader is `src/row_bot/mcp_client/bundles.py`; installing and launching are in `mcp_client/packages.py`. ## What Row-Bot Checks When A Bundle Is Chosen A picked file is staged in Row-Bot's data folder for up to a day and read without being unpacked or run: - **Size**: at most 128 MiB as a file, 512 MiB unpacked, 20,000 files, and a manifest of at most 1 MiB. - **Manifest**: `manifest_version` (or the older `dxt_version`) `0.1` to `0.4`, with `name`, `version`, `description`, `author.name` and `server`. Known optional fields are type-checked; an unknown field refuses the bundle, because what Row-Bot can't read it doesn't accept. - **Server**: `server.type` is `node`, `python` or `binary`; `uv` bundles, which install packages when they start, are read but not run. `server.entry_point` must be inside the archive, and `server.mcp_config` supplies `command`, `args`, `env` and `platform_overrides`. The command must be `node`, `python`, `python3` or a program inside the bundle. - **Platform**: `compatibility.platforms` (all three when absent) must include this computer's (`win32`, `darwin` or `linux`), or the bundle is refused. `compatibility.runtimes` must be well formed but isn't checked against this computer. - **Signature**: see below. ## Settings The Bundle Asks For Each `user_config` entry becomes a field in the setup's **Add your settings** step: | `user_config` | Setup input | | --- | --- | | `title`, `description` (both required) | The field's label and help. | | `type`: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `directory`, `file` | Text, number, yes or no, or a path. | | `sensitive: true` | A secret, kept in the system keychain and never shown again. | | `required` | Whether it must be filled. | | `default` | The starting value; `${HOME}`, `${DESKTOP}`, `${DOCUMENTS}` and `${DOWNLOADS}` become this computer's folders. | `multiple: true` isn't supported. In `mcp_config`, `${__dirname}` is the unpacked bundle and `${user_config.key}` is the person's value, which may fill an argument or an environment variable but never the `command`: a person's value never chooses what runs. Environment variables that change what runs, such as `PATH`, `NODE_OPTIONS` or `LD_PRELOAD`, are refused, except `NODE_PATH` or `PYTHONPATH` inside the bundle. ## Signatures A signed bundle is the zip followed by an `MCPB_SIG_V1` block holding a detached CMS (PKCS #7) signature over the zip, ending with `MCPB_SIG_END`. Row-Bot accepts SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 with RSA or ECDSA keys, and checks that the signature matches the bundle's bytes. - **Signed and matching**: the review shows the name the certificate gives itself and its fingerprint, and says that nobody checked that name. Row-Bot doesn't decide whether the certificate is trusted. - **Unsigned**: the review says Row-Bot can't tell who made it. - **Damaged or not matching**: the bundle is refused.
