A tampered bundle never passes as an unsigned one. ## Install And Launch After the person agrees, the bundle is extracted into a new private folder: only regular files and folders, no links, encrypted entries or path escapes, with the written bytes counted against the limits. Its lock is the file's SHA-256, and its unpacked tree digest is recorded and checked again before every launch; a changed file or folder stops it. `node` bundles run with Row-Bot's managed Node.js (or Node.js on the path), `python` bundles with Row-Bot's own uv-managed Python, and `binary` bundles from inside their folder. Nothing in a bundle runs before consent. ## Bundles From The Registry A Registry record of type `mcpb` gets a recipe only when it gives an https download address and a `fileSha256`; one without a checksum is listed with "Download this bundle from its publisher, then add it from a file". Its consent sheet names the file and its host, "checked against its Registry checksum". Only after the person agrees does Row-Bot re-check the record against the live Registry, download the file through its safe fetcher (https, public addresses, at most 128 MiB), and compare its SHA-256. A bundle that doesn't match is never used or saved: "The bundle didn't match the checksum its Registry record gives, so Row-Bot didn't use it." ## Testing Deterministic tests build bundles in a temporary folder: `tests/subsystem/mcp/test_bundles.py` covers reading, signatures, tampering and contained extraction, and `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_runtimes.py` covers Registry bundles and checksums.

## Sign-In And Client Metadata

Route: /docs/extending/sign-in-and-client-metadata

For developers: how Row-Bot signs in to a hosted app, using its published OAuth client metadata document (CIMD), dynamic client registration or the person's own OAuth app, with a loopback redirect.

# Sign-In And Client Metadata This page is for developers running an MCP server behind OAuth who want Row-Bot to sign in to it, and for anyone reviewing how Row-Bot does it. The code is in `src/row_bot/mcp_client/auth.py`, `application/client_mcp_auth.py` and the `sign_in` step of `integrations/plans.py`. ## Row-Bot's Client Metadata Document Row-Bot has no client secret and no hosted service. Its OAuth client ID is the address of a static Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), `https://row-bot.ai/oauth/client-metadata.json`, published from `docs-site/static/oauth/client-metadata.json`: ```json { "client_id": "https://row-bot.ai/oauth/client-metadata.json", "client_name": "Row-Bot", "client_uri": "https://row-bot.ai", "logo_uri": "https://row-bot.ai/img/brand/row_bot_glyph_256.png", "application_type": "native", "redirect_uris": [ "http://127.0.0.1/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback" ], "grant_types": ["authorization_code", "refresh_token"], "response_types": ["code"], "token_endpoint_auth_method": "none" } ``` It names only loopback redirects, so a sign-in made with it can only return to the computer that started it. It holds no secret or key. ## How Row-Bot Finds Out A Sign-In Is Needed During an agreed setup, the `test` step sends one unauthenticated `initialize` request. A 401 or 403 makes Row-Bot read the server's protected-resource metadata (RFC 9728) and then its authorization server's metadata (RFC 8414), and turns the plan's `sign_in` step on. So a hosted app whose catalog listing says nothing about sign-in can still sign in. These reads are limited to public https addresses and 64 KiB, and happen only inside a setup the person agreed to. ## Which Client Row-Bot Uses 1. **The person's own OAuth app**, when they gave one for this connection before, or when a reviewed recipe says the service needs one (GitHub's OAuth-app way, for example). 2. **CIMD**, when the authorization server's metadata says `client_id_metadata_document_supported` and the sign-in returns to this computer's loopback address. CIMD is preferred when the server supports both. 3. **Dynamic client registration**, when the server has a `registration_endpoint`. Row-Bot registers as a public client named Row-Bot with only its callback address. 4. **Otherwise the setup pauses** at **Add your OAuth app** for a client ID and an optional client secret. The help gives the callback address to register. With a secret, Row-Bot authenticates with `client_secret_post`. The authorization request uses PKCE with S256. A reviewed recipe may set `oauth_scope` to ask for less than everything the server lists. During sign-in Row-Bot checks that the issuer is the expected one, refuses HTTP redirects, contacts public https addresses only, and sends the access token only to the app's own server. ## The Redirect When Row-Bot runs on this computer, the callback is `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback` on the port Row-Bot is using (8080 by default), and the person's browser opens on the same computer. The client metadata lists the address both without a port and with 8080; an authorization server that follows RFC 8252 7.3 accepts any port on a loopback redirect. When Row-Bot is reached through an approved public https address, the callback uses that address, and CIMD isn't used: dynamic registration or the person's own app is. For your own OAuth app, register `http://127.0.0.1/api/v1/settings/mcp/auth/callback` (with a port if your service requires one). ## Tokens Tokens, the client registration and the person's own client secret are saved together for that one connection in Row-Bot's secret store (the system keychain, or Row-Bot's encrypted store where there is none), never in settings files, logs or API responses. They are bound to the connection's name, address and launch; if those change, the person signs in again. When a refresh fails or a token stops working, the app shows **Sign in needed**, and its main action is **Sign in again**. ## Testing `tests/subsystem/integrations/test_sign_in.py` covers discovery, CIMD before dynamic registration, the person's own app, scopes, the expired-sign-in state and the published document. The live GitHub check, `tests/e2e/test_github_live.py`, is opt-in; see [Extend Row-Bot](/docs/extending/#how-apps-and-skills-are-set-up).

## Hosting MCP Apps Views

Route: /docs/extending/mcp-apps

For developers: how Row-Bot shows an app's ui:// view in chat, with the sandboxed frame, its Content-Security-Policy, declared domains, the bridge messages it answers, limits, and calls that go through approvals.

# Hosting MCP Apps Views This page is for developers building an MCP server with interactive views (MCP Apps, spec version `2026-01-26`) or working on Row-Bot itself. For using views, read [Apps in a chat](/docs/chat/#app-views). The server side is `src/row_bot/integrations/views.py`; the frame and bridge are `frontend/src/features/apps/AppViewFrame.tsx` and `view-bridge.ts`. ## Negotiation While **Show app views in chat** is on, Row-Bot's `initialize` request carries the `io.modelcontextprotocol/ui` extension with `mimeTypes: ["text/html;profile=mcp-app"]`. The choice is made when a connection opens; changing the switch doesn't renegotiate an open session. ## Declaring A View - A tool names its view in `_meta.ui.resourceUri` (the older `_meta["ui/resourceUri"]` is read too): a `ui://` URI of at most 512 printable characters. - `_meta.ui.visibility` defaults to `["model", "app"]`. A tool without `"model"` is never offered to the agent; a view can call only tools that include `"app"`. - Row-Bot reads the view with `resources/read` on the app's own connection. It uses the first content item whose `mimeType` is exactly `text/html;profile=mcp-app` and whose `uri` is the one requested, as `text` or base64 `blob`, up to 1 MiB, within 30 seconds. - The content item's `_meta.ui` (not the tool's) supplies `csp` and `prefersBorder`. - A view appears under a tool step that succeeded, for a tool the person accepted, while both view switches are on and the app is on in that chat. It is read again each time its card comes near the screen; nothing is cached. ## The Frame `POST /api/v1/conversations/{id}/views` with `{"call_id": ...}` renders a step's view and returns `frame_url`, `/app-views/{render_id}`, where the render id is 128 random bits. The frame's HTML must be fetched within 120 seconds and is served once; a second request gets 404. The iframe has `sandbox="allow-scripts"` and nothing else, so the view runs in an opaque origin with no access to Row-Bot's page, cookies, storage or API. A second navigation inside the frame closes the view. The response carries `Cache-Control: no-store`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, a `Permissions-Policy` that denies camera, microphone, geolocation, clipboard, USB, serial, payment and display capture, and this policy, where R is the accepted `resourceDomains`: ```text default-src 'none'; script-src 'unsafe-inline' R; style-src 'unsafe-inline' R; img-src data: R; media-src data: R; font-src R; connect-src <connectDomains>; frame-src <frameDomains>; object-src 'none'; base-uri <baseUriDomains>; form-action 'none'; frame-ancestors 'self'; sandbox allow-scripts ``` An empty list becomes `'none'`. No load directive allows `'self'`, which would be Row-Bot's own origin. ## Declared Domains `_meta.ui.csp` may list `resourceDomains`, `connectDomains`, `frameDomains` and `baseUriDomains`. Each value must be an https origin such as `https://cdn.example.com` or `https://*.example.com`, with no port, path or query. Row-Bot silently drops: - IP addresses, single-label names and `localhost`; - private-network names such as `.local`, `.internal`, `.lan`, `.home`, `.corp`, `.test` and `.example`; - wildcard-DNS services such as `nip.io`, `sslip.io` and `localtest.me`; - public suffixes, checked against the bundled Public Suffix List, so `https://*.com` and `https://github.io` are refused. It keeps at most 16 values per kind. The view's card lists the accepted domains: "This view also loads from ...". ## The Bridge The bridge speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over `postMessage`. It accepts messages only from its own frame's window, with origin `null`, up to 1 MiB. | From the view | Row-Bot's answer | | --- | --- | | `ui/initialize` | Host info, capabilities (`serverTools`, `openLinks`, `logging`) and host context: the tool, `theme` (`light` or `dark`), `displayMode: "inline"`, `containerDimensions.maxHeight: 720`, locale, time zone and platform. | | `ui/notifications/initialized` | Sends `ui/notifications/tool-input`, then `ui/notifications/tool-result`, or `ui/notifications/tool-cancelled` when the chat kept no result. | | `ui/notifications/size-changed` | Resizes the frame, between 48 and 720 pixels. | | `tools/call` | Calls one of the app's tools, as described below. Refused before `initialized`. | | `ui/open-link` | Opens an http or https link in the person's browser, only right after a click in the view, at most 3 a minute. | | `ui/request-display-mode` | Always `inline`. | | `ping` | `{}` | | Anything else, such as `ui/message`, `ui/update-model-context` or `resources/read` | `-32601 Method not found`. | Row-Bot sends `ui/notifications/host-context-changed` when the theme changes and `ui/resource-teardown` before it removes a view. A view that hasn't sent `initialized` within 10 seconds is closed. Other notifications, including logging, are ignored. The result a view receives is rebuilt from the chat's text form of the tool result: its text, `isError`, and `structuredContent` when there was one. Images and other non-text content don't reach the view. ## Calls From A View A view's `tools/call` becomes `POST /api/v1/views/{render_id}/tools/call`. Before it runs, Row-Bot checks that: - the tool belongs to the view's own app, includes `"app"` in its visibility, and is turned on for that app; - both view switches are on, and the app is on in that chat and allowed by the chat's agent profile; - the chat's approval mode allows it, through the same rule as the agent's calls. Destructive, high-impact and unknown-effect tools ask in every mode and are refused under **Block**. A routine change the app's access asks about asks under **Ask**, runs under **Auto** and is refused under **Block**. Reads run. When a call asks, the standard approval card appears inside the view's card, as well as wherever approvals appear. The call waits up to 5 minutes without holding a server thread, and no answer counts as a denial. Access is checked again just before the call runs, and the result goes back to the view only, not into the transcript. Limits: 20 calls a minute per view, 64 KiB of arguments, one waiting call per view and three across all views, four app round trips at once, 60 seconds per call, and a 1 MiB result. ## Switches - **Apps Advanced Apps in chats Show app views in chat**: every app. On by default. - **Show views in chat** on an app's page: that app only. On by default when what the person agreed to included a view, and off for apps accepted before views existed. Settings are read and written through `GET` and `PUT /api/v1/integrations/views` and `PUT /api/v1/integrations/views/apps`. ## Testing A View The deterministic fixture `tests/fixtures/mcp_apps/counter_server.py` is a small server with a view; `tests/subsystem/mcp/test_app_views.py` and `frontend/src/features/apps/view-bridge.test.ts` cover the server and the bridge. Test your own view the same way: no live service is needed.

## Operations, Data, And Recovery

Route: /docs/operations/

Back up, restore, update, repair, and uninstall Row-Bot without losing track of local data and credentials.

# Operations, Data, And Recovery Row-Bot is local-first, so operational safety starts with knowing which data directory and workspace are active. Conversations, settings, memory, Knowledge, workflows, documents, designs, code folder records, skills, plugins, logs, channel state, and MCP configuration can live under that directory. Operating-system key stores may hold credentials separately. ## Remote Access And Server Operations Use [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access) for the complete guide to one-time invitations, desktop and compact owner sessions, Tailscale Serve, LAN, SSH forwarding, Docker, HTTPS reverse proxies, browser-local voice, access recovery, and proxy error diagnostics. Use [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker) for pull-first Compose startup, release and digest pins, persistent volumes, offline backup and restore, explicit upgrade and rollback, host Caddy or Tailscale, secret-file mounts, and container-specific Developer boundaries. Remote access remains off by default in ordinary desktop launches. Server operators should back up access state with the rest of the active data directory, keep one worker, publish one canonical origin, terminate remote traffic with HTTPS, and trust only the exact reverse proxy that connects to Row-Bot. ## Back Up **Settings Data Back up and restore** makes a copy of your Row-Bot on this computer, without passwords or sign-ins. Choose **Back up now**; the command palette finds it as "back up". To copy everything by hand instead: 1. Stop running workflows, channels, servers, and active replies. 2. Close Row-Bot so databases are not changing during the copy. 3. Copy the whole active data directory to protected storage. 4. Back up code folders, exported design files, and wiki vaults separately when they live elsewhere. 5. Record the Row-Bot version used with the backup. ## Restore **Restore from backup** on the same page restores a backup made there; it needs the Row-Bot desktop app and lists what to set up again afterwards, such as passwords and sign-ins. To restore a hand-made copy, restore related databases and files as one set while Row-Bot is closed. Point a test launch at the restored directory first, then check conversations, providers, workflows, Knowledge, documents, designs, code folders, plugins, MCP, and channels. Reconnect secrets that were stored in an OS keychain and were not included in the backup. ## Import From Another Assistant **Settings Data Import from another assistant** scans Hermes Agent or OpenClaw data on this computer and lets you choose what to bring in: memories, persona and skills, and, only if you tick it, API keys and tokens. Nothing is written until you confirm the preview. First launch offers it when it finds one of them. The same page's danger zone holds irreversible clean-up, such as removing tracker data. ## Update, Repair, And Uninstall **Settings Updates** shows the version you have, the update **Channel**, and when Row-Bot last checked. **Check for updates** checks now; when an update is available, the sidebar's attention indicator says so and **Remind me later** hides it for a day on this device. Use the supported package or updater flow for your platform. Back up before a major update. Repair may replace application files but should not be treated as a data backup. Uninstalling the application and deleting the local data directory are separate decisions; review both the application location and the data location before removal. ## Logs And Support Use Monitor and the local log folder to diagnose startup, provider, workflow, channel, and background failures. Before sharing diagnostics, remove names, paths, account identifiers, document content, prompts, message content, tokens, and screenshots that expose private data. ## Release-Specific Manual Checks Installer UX, upgrade, repair, uninstall, Windows signing, macOS notarisation, native file dialogs, OS permissions, and clean-machine behaviour require manual testing on release candidates. A successful docs build does not prove those native flows are release-ready.

## Remote Access And Server Mode

Route: /docs/operations/remote-access

Use Row-Bot as one owner from trusted devices through Tailscale, LAN, SSH, Docker, or an HTTPS reverse proxy.

# Remote Access And Server Mode Row-Bot Remote Access lets one owner use the same instance from several trusted browsers. It is a **single-owner, multi-device** system, not a multi-user service or a hostile tenant-isolation boundary. Reachability, authentication, and presentation are separate: - A network route lets a browser reach Row-Bot's neutral connection page. - A one-time invitation authorizes one browser to create a revocable session. - Every authenticated interactive browser represents the same owner. - Desktop or compact presentation changes layout only, never authority. Normal desktop launches remain local-first. They listen on loopback and keep the local owner experience unless you explicitly enable another route. Authenticated server mode is stricter: every browser must connect with a valid session, including a browser on the server itself. ## Configure Remote Access In The App Open **Settings Devices & remote access** from any signed-in owner session, including on a phone. The command palette finds it as "phone" or "connect device". 1. Choose **Connect a phone or computer**. 2. Choose **How will it reach this computer?**: **Tailscale** (private and encrypted HTTPS, recommended), **Same Wi-Fi** (a direct address on your network, over HTTP), **Internet** (from anywhere, through your public link), or **Another address** (a DNS alias, hostname or other browser-facing address you set up yourself, entered as its exact HTTP or HTTPS origin). 3. Choose how long it should **Stay signed in**: **30 days** or **12 hours**. 4. **Scan the code** on the other device, or open the shown address there. Codes work only once; **Show a new code** replaces an expired one. 5. Review the confirmation page on that device, then press **Connect**. The page on the computer then says **Connected**, and **Connect another** starts again. 6. **Your devices** lists every signed-in phone and computer and signs one out. Row-Bot saves a new address, applies its exact Host/origin admission rule immediately, and creates the origin-bound code without a restart. **Same Wi-Fi** first asks to let devices on your network reach Row-Bot, which restarts it to listen on your network. Under **Advanced**, **Network** shows where Row-Bot listens (**This computer only**, or **This computer and my network**) and its **Allowed addresses**, and **Public link** sets up the ngrok tunnel, which opens only when you start it. The choice of routes refreshes from current state when the code is created. Row-Bot refuses a stale or no-longer-reachable selection instead of issuing a misleading link. Saved trusted addresses remain in `access_routes.json` across restarts and appear among the ways to reach this computer. Remove one from **Allowed addresses** when it is no longer needed; new HTTP and WebSocket requests through that exact address are rejected immediately. Removing the address can interrupt current access through it. Enter one exact `http://` or `https://` origin with an optional port, such as `http://row-bot.lan:8080` or `https://row-bot.example.com`. Credentials, paths, queries, fragments, wildcards, malformed ports, and non-HTTP(S) schemes are rejected. A non-default port trusts only that exact authority, not another port. Trusting an address changes only Row-Bot admission and invitation routing. Row-Bot performs no DNS lookup or reachability probe and does not create DNS records, provision TLS, configure a proxy, open a firewall, or change the listen address. HTTP traffic is unencrypted. HTTPS still requires external DNS and TLS setup; a TLS-terminating reverse proxy must also use the existing exact trusted-proxy configuration. Origins supplied through `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_ORIGINS` are listed as **Managed externally** and cannot be edited in the UI. When `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` is set, deployment configuration owns Host admission, so trusted-address add/remove controls are read-only and do not override it. ## Invitations, Sessions, And Layouts | Item | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Invitation | A secret link that expires after 10 minutes and can be consumed once. Opening or previewing it does not connect the device; the recipient must press **Connect**. | | Session | A separate HttpOnly browser credential created after acceptance. Raw session secrets are never placed in the URL. | | Trusted device | A session lasting up to 30 days. An active owner UI checks at startup and every 12 hours, renewing the session to 30 days when it enters the final seven days. | | Temporary access | A session lasting up to 12 hours. | | Desktop layout | The full owner product in its wide-screen presentation. | | Compact layout | The same owner authority in a phone-safe presentation, including every Settings page. Design and Developer panels open as full-screen sheets. | Row-Bot stores only hashed invitation and session secrets in the versioned access database. Sessions survive normal restarts and can be revoked individually. Revoking a device revokes its sessions. An inactive trusted browser can still expire after 30 days; recover by creating a new one-time invitation from a trusted local terminal, SSH session, or container exec. Temporary 12-hour sessions and migrated legacy sessions retain their fixed expiry and do not renew. Row-Bot has no guest or multi-user sharing boundary. Device names, user agents, routes, and layout choices are session metadata, not entitlements. Existing action approval gates continue to govern sensitive tools and operations. Treat an unused invitation like a password. Do not paste it into chat, logs, issue reports, screenshots, shell history you plan to share, or a public URL. ## Choose A Connection Route | Route | Best fit | Important boundary | | --- | --- | --- | | Local desktop | Browser and Row-Bot are on the same computer. | Default desktop mode stays on loopback and does not expose a remote listener. | | Tailscale Serve | Recommended private HTTPS access across your tailnet. | Tailnet membership does not replace a Row-Bot invitation or session. | | Direct LAN | A private, trusted local network. | Remote LAN HTTP is unencrypted and does not provide a secure browser context for microphone capture. | | Trusted hostname or address | An existing exact DNS alias, hostname, or browser-facing IP and port. | Row-Bot trusts only the saved origin; it does not provide DNS, TLS, proxy, firewall, or reachability setup. | | SSH tunnel | An operator can SSH to a remote host and wants no published Row-Bot port. | Keep Row-Bot on loopback and create the invitation for the workstation-facing forwarded origin. | | Docker | A headless, isolated, reproducible instance. | The supplied Compose file publishes to host loopback by default and persists `/data`. | | HTTPS reverse proxy | An operator owns DNS, TLS, proxy configuration, backups, and ingress policy. | Trust only the exact proxy address or CIDR that connects to Row-Bot. | An active route means the connection page is reachable. It does not mean the browser is trusted. ## Tailscale Serve Tailscale Serve is the recommended desktop route because it provides a private HTTPS origin without changing Row-Bot's default bind address. Row-Bot does not install Tailscale, sign you in, enable Funnel, reset the complete Serve configuration, change firewall rules, or overwrite an unrelated route. Status checks and planning are read-only. Enabling a route requires you to review the exact private Serve change, accept the third-party disclosure, and confirm it in the UI. Row-Bot refuses to mutate when Funnel is active, a conflicting route exists, ownership cannot be verified, or the Tailscale CLI outcome is ambiguous. It records ownership only after it verifies the exact route it created, and it removes only that unchanged owned route. After a verified enable or disable, Row-Bot asks its launcher to restart the app. That restart activates the matching proxy policy: - only loopback connections from the local Tailscale proxy are trusted; - only the verified owned `.ts.net` host and HTTPS origin are added; - the owned route must still target this exact Row-Bot app port. If the launcher is unavailable, the UI tells you to restart Row-Bot manually. A manually managed Tailscale or reverse-proxy route is not treated as Row-Bot-owned; configure its public URL, allowed host, and exact proxy trust explicitly. After Tailscale reports **Active Owned**, create the invitation for its verified private origin. The recipient still needs the one-time invitation and resulting Row-Bot session. ## Direct LAN Use **Allow local-network connections** only on a network you trust. The launcher restarts Row-Bot after the durable listen setting changes. Anyone who can reach the port can see the neutral connection page, but cannot use the application without a valid session. LAN HTTP is unencrypted. Prefer Tailscale or an operator-managed HTTPS origin on shared, guest, workplace, or otherwise untrusted networks. Row-Bot does not change the host firewall. ## SSH Tunnel Start Row-Bot on loopback: ```bash row-bot serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 ``` Forward a workstation port: ```bash ssh -N -L 18080:127.0.0.1:8080 user@row-bot-host ``` Create the invitation for the origin the browser will actually use: ```bash row-bot access invite \ --layout desktop \ --origin http://127.0.0.1:18080 ``` ## Advanced / Managed Deployments Environment variables and CLI flags remain useful when deployment tooling must own policy. `ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_ORIGINS` entries are visible but read-only in Settings. Setting `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` makes Host admission externally managed and disables trusted-address mutation in the UI; durable UI addresses never override that explicit policy. ### Authenticated Server Mode `row-bot serve` starts one authenticated headless instance. It defaults to loopback, one worker, no tray, no splash, no opened browser, and no automatic Ollama startup. For a host-installed HTTPS reverse proxy: ```bash row-bot serve \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8080 \ --public-url https://row-bot.example.com \ --allowed-host row-bot.example.com \ --trusted-proxy 127.0.0.1/32 ``` The equivalent core environment settings are: ```text ROW_BOT_DEPLOYMENT_MODE=server ROW_BOT_PUBLIC_URL=https://row-bot.example.com ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=row-bot.example.com ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=127.0.0.1/32 ROW_BOT_WORKERS=1 ``` Use the address that actually connects from the proxy to Row-Bot. Do not trust every private address, a whole Docker bridge range, or caller-supplied forwarding headers. Do not buffer the event stream (`/api/v1/events`, `text/event-stream`) and terminate remote traffic with HTTPS. The reviewed [Caddy example](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/deploy/reverse-proxy/Caddyfile.example) and [systemd service](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/deploy/systemd/row-bot.service.example) are starting points, not substitutes for operator-owned firewall, rate-limit, logging, backup, and recovery policy. The deprecated `row-bot --server --no-open` form remains compatible, but new scripts and services should use `row-bot serve`. ## Docker The supplied Docker image contains the complete supported server feature set: all canonical Python extras, matching headless Playwright Chromium, native media libraries, `uv`/`uvx`, and pinned Node.js with `node`/`npm`/`npx`. It does not contain invitations, sessions, credentials, downloaded voice models, arbitrary MCP servers, or Tailscale. Compose publishes `127.0.0.1:8080` by default and persists private state and explicit model/runtime downloads under `/data`. Every browser must claim an invitation, including a browser on the Docker host. Docker bridge and gateway addresses never grant owner identity. Follow [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker) for the pull-first public runbook, and use the repository's [Docker operator notes](https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot/blob/main/deploy/docker/README.md) when building from source. The public guide covers: - invitation bootstrap with `docker compose exec`; - intentional LAN or HTTPS publication; - multiple isolated instances; - health and readiness checks; - read-only secret files; - backups, upgrades, restore, and rollback; - trusted-session renewal and inactive-session recovery; - browser, MCP runtime, local-model cache, and headless feature boundaries. Never mount the host Docker socket merely to satisfy a tool or MCP server. ## Voice From A Remote Browser Local browser voice uses the requesting browser's microphone and speaker. The browser sends bounded audio to Row-Bot for transcription with the selected local STT engine: Whisper by default, or SenseVoice after its explicit installation. Row-Bot returns local Kokoro audio to that same browser. A headless server or container does not need access to the host microphone or speakers. Browsers permit microphone capture on `localhost` or in a secure HTTPS context. Plain HTTP on a remote LAN address is insufficient. Use Tailscale HTTPS or a correctly configured HTTPS reverse proxy for remote dictation or talk. Whisper, SenseVoice, and Kokoro model installation remains an explicit owner action and can use several gigabytes of persistent cache. SenseVoice alone is an approximately 940 MB ModelScope download and is unavailable on Intel macOS. OpenAI Realtime voice is a separate provider/network feature; local browser voice does not silently fall back to it. ## Offline Access Management And Recovery Use a trusted local terminal, SSH session, or `docker compose exec`: ```bash row-bot access invite --layout desktop --origin https://row-bot.example.com row-bot access invite --layout compact --temporary --origin https://row-bot.example.com row-bot access list row-bot access revoke DEVICE_ID row-bot access revoke SESSION_ID --session row-bot access revoke-all --yes row-bot access doctor ``` `list` and `doctor` never print reusable session secrets. Invitation commands are the only commands that print a raw one-time link. If every owner session is lost, create a new owner invitation from a trusted terminal. Back up the complete active `ROW_BOT_DATA_DIR` while Row-Bot is stopped. It contains conversations, configuration, instance identity, invitations, devices, sessions, and other private state; operating-system keyring credentials may require a separate recovery plan. ## Troubleshooting - **`untrusted_forwarding_headers`**: a proxy supplied forwarding headers from an address Row-Bot does not trust. For a Row-Bot-owned Tailscale route, restart once if the UI reports that restart is required. For an operator proxy, set only its exact connecting address in `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`. Do not fix this by trusting a broad network. - **`unexpected_host`**: on a desktop launch, open **Settings Devices & remote access**, add the exact browser-facing origin (as **Another address** when connecting a device, or under **Advanced Network Allowed addresses**), and retry without restarting. In a managed deployment, the host may instead be missing from `ROW_BOT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`, or the proxy may have forwarded a different host. - **Origin or invitation mismatch**: create the invitation for the exact browser-facing scheme, host, and port. Do not reuse an invitation after changing routes. - **Tailscale conflict or unowned route**: inspect the existing Serve configuration. Row-Bot will not reset or overwrite it. - **Phone reaches the page but cannot use Row-Bot**: reachability is working; create or reclaim the correct invitation and confirm the device was not revoked. - **Remote microphone unavailable**: use HTTPS, grant microphone permission in that browser, and install the local voice model explicitly. - **Server starts but is not ready**: check `/healthz`, `/readyz`, local logs, and `row-bot access doctor`. For command lookup, see the generated [CLI reference](/docs/reference/generated/cli) and [environment reference](/docs/reference/generated/environment-and-config).

## Docker And VPS Operations

Route: /docs/operations/docker

Run one persistent Row-Bot server with Docker Compose, private host access, or an operator-managed HTTPS edge.

# Docker And VPS Operations The official container runs one **single-owner, multi-device** Row-Bot instance. It is not a multi-user service or a hostile tenant-isolation boundary. Every browser, including one on the Docker host, must claim a one-time invitation before it receives a revocable owner session. The default Compose topology publishes only `127.0.0.1:8080`, runs the application as UID/GID 10001 with a read-only root filesystem, and keeps private state in separate named data and encryption-key volumes. It does not mount the Docker socket, host devices, a desktop display, or host audio. ## Prerequisites - Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with Linux containers and Docker Compose. - Enough disk for the full image plus the `/data` volume. Models, managed runtimes, browser outputs, and caches can grow after explicit use; Row-Bot does not promise one fixed capacity figure. - For public VPS access: Linux, Docker Compose 2.24.4 or newer, DNS you control, and a host-managed HTTPS proxy or Tailscale installation. Release images are built from tagged source in GitHub Actions with the locked dependency set. Native amd64 and arm64 jobs run the isolated authenticated-container smoke before the release manifest is created, and the registry exposes a digest for immutable pins. The smoke uses bounded request timeouts and requires two consecutive readiness samples; it retries only safe GET probes, never repeats a state-changing POST, and limits failure output to redacted container state and log tails. ## Download A Release-Pinned Compose File You do not need to clone the repository. Choose a released version, create a private deployment directory, and download the Compose file from the same tag: ```bash mkdir -p row-bot-docker cd row-bot-docker curl -fsSLo compose.yaml \ "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/docker/compose.yaml" docker buildx imagetools inspect "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" docker compose -f compose.yaml config ``` Replace `X.Y.Z` with a release that lists the Row-Bot container in GitHub Packages. A source tag can exist without a published container, so confirm the image before starting. Pull requests and manually dispatched container checks verify builds but do not publish them; publishing happens only after a GitHub Release is published. If the registry reports `manifest unknown` for the version you chose, select a release with a container or use [Build From Source](#build-from-source). Keep `ROW_BOT_VERSION`, the downloaded file, and `ROW_BOT_IMAGE` aligned. The Compose default is `ghcr.io/siddsachar/row-bot:latest`, but an explicit version is easier to audit and roll back. Stable releases also update `latest`; prereleases do not. For an immutable image pin, replace the tag with the digest published for that release: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml config ``` ## Account Credential Persistence Is Automatic Headless containers do not have a desktop keyring. On every `docker compose up`, a short-lived, network-disabled initializer creates a random `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` only when the project-scoped `row_bot_secrets` volume is empty. The application receives that volume read-only and uses the key to encrypt ChatGPT/Codex tokens and other owner-entered secrets under `/data/secure-secrets`. There is no key to create or environment value to set for the normal Compose path. Keep both named volumes for restart, container replacement, upgrade, and rollback, and back up the key separately from `/data`. Advanced unattended deployments can replace the generated key volume with an operator-managed read-only directory as described in [Read-Only Secret Files](#read-only-secret-files). ## First Start And Owner Invitation A fresh `up` pulls the image only when it is absent locally, creates the data and encryption-key volumes, initializes the key without network access, and starts the foreground server: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d docker compose -f compose.yaml ps curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz ``` The unauthenticated root shows a neutral connection flow. Create the first invitation from a private terminal; the output is a one-time secret: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \ row-bot access invite --layout desktop --origin http://127.0.0.1:8080 ``` Open the printed URL, review the confirmation, and select **Connect**. Use `--layout compact` for phone presentation. Both layouts grant the same owner authority. Useful secret-free checks are: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot row-bot access list docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot row-bot access doctor --host 127.0.0.1 docker compose -f compose.yaml logs --tail 200 row-bot ``` Do not paste invitation URLs, cookies, provider credentials, or unredacted logs into issues or chat. ## Finish Setup And Install Private Knowledge Search First launch is the same in desktop, source, and Docker installations: answer **How should Row-Bot think?** to choose your first model. Private knowledge search uses **Mixedbread Embed Large v1**, a separate local model for semantic memory and document search, as a 675 MB download you start from Settings -> Documents (Setup Center links there). The download requires internet access to Hugging Face and does not upload documents or memories. In Docker, the downloaded files live in the `/data` cache, so the named volume preserves them across restarts and container replacement. Install it for the recommended semantic search experience. Until then, Row-Bot still works and uses bounded lexical and graph fallback; install the model from [Settings -> Documents](/docs/settings/documents) under **Search model files**. After changing an embedding provider or model, rebuild the document and memory vectors from this screen. A cloud embedding provider is a separate opt-in choice and sends the indexed text to that provider; the recommended default stays local after the initial download. ## Stop, Restart, Reboot, And Replace Normal stop and start retain the container and named volume: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml stop row-bot docker compose -f compose.yaml start row-bot ``` `restart: unless-stopped` lets an existing service return when the Docker daemon starts after a host reboot. After every reboot, verify `ps`, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, and an existing authenticated browser. Replacing only the container preserves the same instance identity, settings, sessions, conversations, and selected caches in `/data`: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d --force-recreate row-bot ``` ## Multiple Isolated Instances Use a different Compose project name and host port for each instance. Compose project names isolate the containers, networks, and named data and encryption-key volumes: ```bash docker compose --project-name row-bot-main \ -f compose.yaml up -d ROW_BOT_HOST_PORT=8081 docker compose --project-name row-bot-lab \ -f compose.yaml up -d ``` Create invitations for `http://127.0.0.1:8080` and `http://127.0.0.1:8081`, respectively. Every project automatically receives its own data and encryption-key volumes. Do not copy one instance's access database or encryption key into another unless you are deliberately restoring that same instance. Each fresh instance has a different identity, so its cookies and owner sessions remain isolated even when the hostname is the same. ## Consistent Offline Backup Treat a backup as private user data. Stop the service before copying the whole volume so related SQLite files are one consistent set. Use a disposable helper container to create archives; do not use `docker compose cp` for the complete `/data` tree because model caches can contain symbolic links that a Windows host cannot reproduce. The helper has no network, receives the source volumes read-only, and adds only the capability needed to read every file in the stopped volume: ```bash backup_dir="$(pwd)/backups/row-bot-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)" mkdir -p "$backup_dir" docker compose -f compose.yaml stop row-bot row_bot_container="$(docker compose -f compose.yaml ps -a -q row-bot)" docker run --rm \ --network none \ --read-only \ --user 0:0 \ --cap-drop ALL \ --cap-add DAC_READ_SEARCH \ --security-opt no-new-privileges \ --volumes-from "${row_bot_container}:ro" \ --mount "type=bind,src=${backup_dir},dst=/backup" \ --entrypoint sh \ "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" \ -c 'set -eu; tar -C /data -czf /backup/data.tar.gz .; tar -C /run/secrets -czf /backup/secrets.tar.gz ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY' docker compose -f compose.yaml start row-bot ``` Run the final `start` command even if archive creation reports an error. On Windows PowerShell, use `$backupDir = (New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "backups\\row-bot-$((Get-Date).ToUniversalTime().ToString('yyyyMMddTHHmmssZ'))").FullName`, `$rowBotContainer = docker compose -f compose.yaml ps -a -q row-bot`, backticks instead of backslashes for line continuation, `$backupDir` in the bind mount, and `$env:ROW_BOT_IMAGE` as the image value. The archive work still runs inside Linux and therefore preserves cache symlinks. Encrypt and protect both `data.tar.gz` and `secrets.tar.gz` with your normal backup system. Record the image tag and digest beside them. Encrypted server credentials under `/data/secure-secrets` are usable only with the matching `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`; protect both archives. Other credentials supplied through an operator-managed read-only directory need their own recovery procedure. Test a restore under a different Compose project name and port. This creates a separate named volume and does not overwrite the live instance: ```bash restore_backup_dir="$(cd ./backups/RESTORE_SET && pwd)" docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml \ create secret-store-init row-bot restore_app_container="$(docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml ps -a -q row-bot)" restore_init_container="$(docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml ps -a -q secret-store-init)" docker run --rm \ --network none \ --read-only \ --user 0:0 \ --cap-drop ALL \ --cap-add CHOWN \ --cap-add FOWNER \ --cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE \ --security-opt no-new-privileges \ --volumes-from "${restore_app_container}" \ --mount "type=bind,src=${restore_backup_dir},dst=/backup,readonly" \ --entrypoint sh \ "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" \ -c 'set -eu; tar -C /data -xzf /backup/data.tar.gz' docker run --rm \ --network none \ --read-only \ --user 0:0 \ --cap-drop ALL \ --cap-add CHOWN \ --cap-add FOWNER \ --cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE \ --security-opt no-new-privileges \ --volumes-from "${restore_init_container}" \ --mount "type=bind,src=${restore_backup_dir},dst=/backup,readonly" \ --entrypoint sh \ "${ROW_BOT_IMAGE}" \ -c 'set -eu; tar -C /run/secrets -xzf /backup/secrets.tar.gz' docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml up -d curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:18080/readyz docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \ row-bot access doctor --host 127.0.0.1 ``` Set `ROW_BOT_IMAGE` to the recorded image before restoring. On PowerShell, resolve the backup directory with `$restoreBackupDir = (Resolve-Path '.\\backups\\RESTORE_SET').Path`, capture the two container IDs with `$restoreAppContainer` and `$restoreInitContainer`, and use those variables in the same helper commands. Inspect the restored data and authentication before changing any proxy or production route. Remove the isolated project with `docker compose --project-name row-bot-restore -f compose.yaml down --volumes` only after you have finished the restore test. ## Explicit Upgrade And Rollback Upgrades are never automatic. Take an offline backup, choose the new version or digest, pull it explicitly, recreate, and run checks: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml pull row-bot docker compose -f compose.yaml up -d row-bot docker compose -f compose.yaml ps curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \ row-bot access doctor --host 127.0.0.1 ``` Also verify an existing browser session and a normal streamed response. For rollback, use the previous image digest with its matching pre-upgrade data backup in an isolated project first. Database changes can make an old image incompatible with state already opened by a newer one. ## Read-Only Secret Files The default stack already provides encrypted persistence for secrets entered in the UI. For centrally managed or pre-provisioned deployments, you can instead keep one allowlisted setting value per file in an absolute private host directory outside the repository. This override replaces the automatic key volume, so the directory must also contain `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY`. Download the example override from the same release tag: ```bash curl -fsSLo compose.secrets.yaml.example \ "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/docker/compose.secrets.yaml.example" sudo install -d -o 10001 -g 10001 -m 0700 "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR" openssl rand -hex 32 | sudo tee \ "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY" >/dev/null sudo chown 10001:10001 \ "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY" sudo chmod 0400 \ "$ROW_BOT_SECRETS_HOST_DIR/ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY" docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.secrets.yaml.example config docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.secrets.yaml.example up -d ``` Restrict the host directory to the Docker operator and container UID/GID 10001. The override mounts only `/run/secrets:ro`; it does not put values into Compose environment, labels, command lines, or image layers. Externally managed provider and channel values remain read-only in Settings and are never copied into `/data`. `ROW_BOT_SECRET_STORE_KEY` is different: it is a 32-byte master key encoded as exactly 64 hexadecimal characters. The default initializer generates it automatically in the project-scoped key volume; the override above makes you its operator. When a desktop keyring is unavailable, Row-Bot uses it to encrypt in-app OAuth tokens and other owner-entered secrets under `/data/secure-secrets`. This allows ChatGPT/Codex and other rotating OAuth credentials to survive a process restart or container replacement without placing the tokens in environment variables. The master key itself remains only in `/run/secrets` and is never copied into `/data`. Keep the same key for backup, restore, upgrade, and rollback. A missing key leaves newly entered credentials session-only; an invalid or changed key fails closed and cannot decrypt, replace, or delete existing encrypted records. There is no automatic key rotation. To replace a lost key, reconnect the affected accounts and re-enter secrets after deliberately starting with an empty encrypted secret directory. ## Build From Source Source builds are opt-in and require a repository checkout. The build override changes only the image source; the base file remains authoritative for runtime and security settings: ```bash git clone https://github.com/siddsachar/row-bot.git cd row-bot docker compose \ -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml \ -f deploy/docker/compose.build.yaml \ build row-bot docker compose \ -f deploy/docker/compose.yaml \ -f deploy/docker/compose.build.yaml \ up -d ``` Record the source revision and resulting image digest before relying on a source build. ## Linux VPS With Host Caddy This topology uses host networking only in the VPS override. Row-Bot binds `127.0.0.1:8080`; host Caddy terminates HTTPS on ports 80/443 and connects from IPv4 loopback. Nothing publishes container port 8080 externally. 1. Point the dedicated DNS name at the VPS. 2. Allow inbound TCP 80/443 in the host and provider firewalls; do not expose 8080. 3. Install and operate Caddy on the host. 4. Download the release-matched override and Caddy example: ```bash curl -fsSLo compose.vps.yaml \ "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/docker/compose.vps.yaml" curl -fsSLo Caddyfile.row-bot \ "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/siddsachar/row-bot/v${ROW_BOT_VERSION}/deploy/reverse-proxy/Caddyfile.example" ``` Set the exact browser-facing origin and host, then validate the merged configuration: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml config docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml up -d curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/readyz ``` The override sets `ROW_BOT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS=127.0.0.1/32` exactly. Replace the example hostname in `Caddyfile.row-bot`, integrate that site block into the host's Caddy configuration, then validate and reload Caddy using the host package's service procedure. Do not broaden proxy trust to a private range or accept caller-supplied forwarding metadata. Create the invitation for the exact HTTPS origin: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml exec row-bot \ row-bot access invite --layout desktop \ --origin https://row-bot.example.com ``` From an external browser, confirm the HTTPS connection page, claim the invitation, keep the UI open through a streamed response, and verify its event stream stays connected. Reboot the VPS during a maintenance window and repeat DNS, TLS, readiness, authenticated-session, and streaming checks. ## Host-Managed Tailscale Serve Tailscale runs on the Linux host, not in the Row-Bot container. Use the VPS override so host Tailscale reaches Row-Bot over exact loopback, but do not install or invoke the Tailscale CLI inside the container. Set the host's actual private HTTPS name: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.vps.yaml up -d sudo tailscale serve --bg http://127.0.0.1:8080 tailscale serve status ``` Create an invitation for that exact `https://...ts.net` origin. Tailnet membership supplies private reachability; it does not replace Row-Bot's invitation, session, or revocation controls. The container neither contains nor controls the host Tailscale CLI, Funnel, login, firewall, or route lifecycle. ## Trusted Sessions And Recovery A trusted browser session lasts up to 30 days. While an authenticated owner UI remains active, the browser checks at startup and every 12 hours. In the final seven days, the server atomically renews that trusted session to 30 days. Temporary 12-hour sessions and migrated legacy sessions never renew. An inactive trusted browser can still expire after 30 days. If all sessions are lost, recover only from a trusted host terminal or SSH session: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml exec row-bot \ row-bot access invite --layout desktop --origin YOUR_EXACT_ORIGIN ``` Revoked, expired, or device-revoked credentials stay invalid. ## Developer And Headless Boundaries There are three distinct Developer execution cases: 1. **Row-Bot installed on a host:** Docker Sandbox can use the host's supported Docker runtime when it is available. Local mode remains an explicit workspace choice. 2. **The official Row-Bot application container:** Developer Docker Sandbox is unavailable and fails closed. The image contains no Docker daemon or CLI, and you must not mount the host Docker socket. Local mode can use only a workspace path you explicitly mount into the application container. 3. **An approved Custom Tool inside the application container:** risky approved execution deliberately uses Local mode inside that same container against the selected visible path. It is not a nested Docker sandbox and is not a silent fallback from a requested Docker workspace. The container has no native tray/window, native desktop Computer Use, physical host microphone or speaker, camera, display server, or GPU by default. Browser-local voice and bundled headless browser automation remain available. Selected local models and runtimes are explicit downloads into `/data`; cache growth depends on what the owner installs and uses. ## Remove The Deployment Ordinary removal keeps private state: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml down ``` To delete both named volumes and all instance state deliberately, first verify the Compose project and backup, then run: ```bash docker compose -f compose.yaml down --volumes ``` Those volume deletions remove both private data and the generated encryption key and are not recoverable unless you have a tested backup. External secret directories and backup directories are separate and are never removed by these Compose commands.

## Privacy And Safety

Route: /docs/privacy-safety/

Understand local data, provider calls, credentials, approvals, channels, MCP, plugins, and sharing.

# Privacy And Safety Row-Bot is local-first: the app and its data live on your machine. Local-first does not mean every feature is offline. Hosted models, web search, browser actions, account tools, channels, MCP servers, plugins, realtime voice, and media providers can send data outside the app when you configure and use them. ## Local Data Conversations, memories, documents, workflows, logs, designs, code folder records, skills, plugins, Buddy assets, and settings are stored in the active local Row-Bot data directory. Buddy's native overlay reuses the selected conversation and does not create a second transcript store. ## External Calls External calls happen when you choose or enable something that needs them: hosted models, subscription providers, API providers, web search, browser automation, account tools, messaging channels, MCP servers, plugin tools, realtime voice, and media generation. OpenRouter requests identify Row-Bot as the app making them (its website address and name, in the headers OpenRouter asks apps to send), which lets OpenRouter show Row-Bot in its public app rankings; these headers add no user, prompt or account data. Computer Use is a distinct opt-in boundary. Row-Bot downloads the pinned Cua Driver only after an explicit Install or Repair action, verifies the selected archive, and requires the current telemetry disclosure before any executable invocation. The reviewed 0.20.0 upstream telemetry includes pseudonymous identifiers and bounded product, platform, client, tool/outcome, duration/output, aggregate usage, permission, and lifecycle categories; its tagged event builders exclude prompts, tool arguments/results, typed text, screenshots, accessibility trees, app/window names, URLs, paths, raw values, and raw errors. See [Computer Use](/docs/computer-use/) for the full boundary. ## Credentials Enter credentials only on the relevant Settings page or in the provider sign-in flow. Row-Bot stores secrets in the operating system key store when available and keeps local metadata for status and diagnostics. An explicitly configured server deployment can use a read-only external master-key file to encrypt owner-entered secrets in its persistent data directory; see [Docker And VPS Operations](/docs/operations/docker#read-only-secret-files). ## Remote Access Remote Access is single-owner and multi-device. A Tailscale, LAN, SSH, Docker, or reverse-proxy route provides reachability only; each non-local browser still needs a one-time invitation and a revocable Row-Bot session. Every authenticated interactive browser has full owner authority. Phone/tablet and computer choices select compact or desktop presentation only; device metadata and screen size are not permission boundaries. Row-Bot does not provide guest or multi-user sharing. Invitation links expire after 10 minutes and work once, but should still be treated like passwords until they expire. Row-Bot stores only hashed invitation and session secrets. Session credentials use HttpOnly cookies and are not placed in URLs. Prefer Tailscale or HTTPS for remote access. Plain LAN HTTP is unencrypted and does not support a remote browser microphone. For an operator-managed proxy, allow only the canonical browser-facing origin and trust only the exact address that connects from the proxy to Row-Bot. Never resolve a forwarding-header error by trusting every private address or a whole container network. See [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access) for layouts, lifetimes, revocation, Tailscale ownership, server mode, Docker, and recovery. ## Approvals Use approvals to review file writes, command execution, browser actions, account actions, channel sends, MCP calls, plugin tools, code folder changes, and other sensitive actions. Deny anything that does not match your request. Approvals wait until you answer; they no longer expire on their own, unless a workflow step sets its own time limit. Every waiting approval shows in its conversation, in the sidebar's attention indicator and on Overview, with **Approve** and **Deny** in place, so background work can't slip past you. Each tool result records whether approval was needed, given or denied, and a denied action never runs. Approval mode is policy, not a model choice: blocked actions stay blocked, ask-mode actions wait for you, and auto-approved actions follow the configured policy. Some prompts include a short model-written reason for readability, but the underlying approval gate and action details are system-controlled. ## Sharing Logs Or Screenshots Before sharing logs, screenshots, documents, thread exports, or review packages, check for names, file paths, account names, message contents, tokens, private documents, or misleading real data. ## Safer Defaults - Start with local models when privacy matters most. - Keep channels, MCP, and plugins disabled until needed. - Keep Computer Use disabled until a local interactive task needs native application control. - Keep Remote Access off until another trusted device needs it; use the narrowest route and the appropriate layout. - Use narrow workspaces for file tools. - Review approvals before external or destructive actions. - Keep a final human review step before publishing screenshots or docs built from a personal app state.

## Troubleshooting

Route: /docs/troubleshooting/

Resolve setup, model, chat, approval, workflow, design, code folder, Knowledge, Monitor, app, skill, channel, account, catalog, voice, and Buddy issues.

# Troubleshooting Start with what Row-Bot already tells you. The sidebar's attention indicator appears when something needs you, Overview's **Needs you** lists it, and [Monitor](/docs/monitor/) shows every health check with a one-click fix. Most issues fall into one of four categories: setup is incomplete, a provider or tool is off, the wrong model is selected, or Row-Bot is waiting for your approval. ## Setup Problems - If Row-Bot keeps opening setup, finish **How should Row-Bot think?** or choose **Set up later**. Open Setup Center from Overview or the command palette to continue optional setup. - Check Settings Providers and Settings Models before troubleshooting a conversation. - Check Settings System if local files, browser automation, or command execution are involved, and Settings Devices & remote access for other devices or the public link. - For native application control, open the Computer Use setup in Settings System and resolve its driver or operating-system permission status before retrying. ## Model Problems - Refresh the provider in Settings Providers, then refresh the catalog in Settings Models. - A model marked **Unavailable** in a picker says why; reconnecting its provider usually fixes it. - Choose a tool-capable model for workflows, designs, code folders, and multi-step tool use. - For local and custom endpoints, use enough context for Row-Bot's instructions and tool schemas; lower the **Reading limit** in Settings Models on smaller computers. - If reasoning choices are missing, rejected, or reset, use the active model's conditional control or `/reasoning`, then follow [Reasoning Controls](/docs/chat/reasoning-controls#troubleshooting). ## Chat, Tool, And Approval Problems - Check the model picker, the composer's **Mode** (Agent or Chat only), the conversation's agent profile, its **Approvals** setting, and the enabled tools. - If an action is waiting, approve or deny it in the conversation, from the sidebar's attention indicator, or from Overview. Approvals wait until you answer. - If a step shows as skipped, it was denied and did not run. - Ask Row-Bot to explain the last tool result if the transcript is unclear. - If Computer Use is paused, choose Resume only after reviewing the target; if its lease is busy, stop or finish the active native task first. ## Workflow Problems - Confirm the workflow is enabled, and that an earlier run isn't still waiting for approval: while one waits, the next scheduled run is skipped. - Run it once with **Run** before trusting a schedule. - Check delivery defaults and the channel's status in Monitor. ## Design And Code Folder Problems - Designs: give a clearer goal, audience and length, and attach references. Exports use the last saved version. - Code folders: check that the folder is listed under **Working on** in the conversation's details card. Choosing or cloning a folder needs the Row-Bot desktop app. - Review commands and changes before approving or importing them. ## Knowledge And Monitor Problems - If Knowledge is empty, turn on memory in Settings Memory or add documents in Settings Documents. - If a memory is wrong, edit, merge or archive it in Home Knowledge. - Use Monitor's **Needs attention**, **History** and **Logs** for background issues, and **Copy diagnosis report** when asking for help. ## Apps And Skills An app that isn't ready shows one status and one fix: the main action on its page in **Settings Apps**, also offered in Overview's **Needs you**. | Status | What it means | Do this | | --- | --- | --- | | **Sign in needed** | The app needs a sign-in, or its saved sign-in stopped working. | **Sign in**, or **Sign in again**. | | **Key needed** | It needs a key or token. | **Add key**. | | **Finish setup** | Setup stopped before the end, waiting for a setting, the actions to allow, or something it needs to run. | **Continue setup**. | | **Working...** | Row-Bot is finishing your last change. | Wait a moment. | | **Needs attention** | The connection failed, or Row-Bot couldn't confirm your last change. | **Fix**, or **Retry**. | | **Off** | You turned it off. | **Turn on**. | | **Removed** | A package was removed and its saved data kept. | **Delete saved data** when you no longer need it. | - **Finishing your last change... Retry**: Row-Bot couldn't confirm that a change finished, for example because it closed part-way. **Retry** checks what happened and never repeats the change. - **Open _program_, then check again**: the app works with a program on this computer, such as Blender. Open the program and its add-on, then choose **Check again**. - **Install Docker Desktop, then try again**, or **Docker Desktop isn't running on this computer**: the app runs as a container image. Install or open Docker Desktop, or choose another way to connect on the app's page. - **_App_ needs your own OAuth app to sign in**: the service accepts only an OAuth app you create. Create one at the service, register the callback address the step shows, and paste its **Client ID** (and **Client secret (optional)**, if it has one). - If Google asks you to sign in every 7 days, your Google app is still in **Testing**; see [Google sign-ins in Testing last 7 days](/docs/integrations/accounts#google-sign-ins-in-testing-last-7-days). - If an app's tools never appear in chat, check that it is **Ready**, that it is checked in the chat's **+ Apps**, that the chat's agent profile allows it, and that **Apps Advanced Apps in chats** has **Use apps** on and offers app tools. - Channels and accounts are apps too (for example **Apps Telegram** or **Apps Google**); **Open** on the app's page opens their own settings. A stopped channel shows **Restart** in Monitor, and an account whose sign-in expired shows **Reconnect** there. - Skills need to be in **Your skills** in **Settings Skills**, turned on, and relevant to the prompt; you can also call one with its slash command. ### Catalogs And Proxies - **Couldn't update. The last copy is still used.**: the catalog couldn't be reached. Search keeps working with the last copy; choose **Update** again later. - Behind a proxy, Row-Bot sends catalog updates and **Search online catalogs** through the proxy set in Windows or macOS settings or in the `HTTPS_PROXY` environment variable. It doesn't run automatic proxy configuration (PAC) scripts, so set the proxy's address itself. - Logos, bundles downloaded from the Registry and app sign-ins connect directly, not through the proxy, so they fail on a network that allows only proxied traffic. ### Windows Connectors, Composio And App Views - **Windows connectors** appear in **Apps Advanced Catalogs** only on Windows builds that have Windows' On-device Agent Registry (Insider build 26220.7344 or later, with **Experimental agentic features** on). Choose **Update** to list them. - **Composio** isn't searched until you turn on **Use Composio** in **Apps Advanced Catalogs** and agree to its disclosure: it is a separate service, with its own account, that keeps requests and results for up to a year by default. Turning it off doesn't remove a Composio connection you made; remove that on its page. - **App views** show only under a step that succeeded, for an app that has views, while **Show app views in chat** (in **Apps Advanced**) and **Show views in chat** on the app's page are on and the app is on in that chat. "This view didn't start" or "Views are busy" usually clears with **Open again**. ## Remote Access And Server Mode - If the browser shows `untrusted_forwarding_headers`, a proxy supplied forwarding metadata from an address Row-Bot does not trust. Restart after enabling a Row-Bot-owned Tailscale route. For another proxy, configure only its exact connecting address or CIDR; do not trust a broad network. - If the browser shows `unexpected_host`, add the exact canonical browser-facing host and verify the proxy preserves it. - If a code cannot be used, create it for the exact scheme, host, and port currently used by that browser. Expired, used and stale-route codes must be recreated. - If Tailscale reports a conflict, Funnel, or an unowned route, inspect that configuration manually. Row-Bot deliberately refuses to reset or overwrite it. - If a remote microphone is unavailable, use `localhost` or HTTPS, grant browser permission, and install the local voice model explicitly. - Run `row-bot access doctor` for a secret-free server and route safety report. The full route, authentication, Docker, proxy, and recovery guidance is in [Remote Access And Server Mode](/docs/operations/remote-access). ## Voice And Buddy - Check microphone and output device selection and permissions. - Use Dictate before Talk if you need review. - Check provider readiness for realtime voice. - If docked Buddy is missing, enable **Show Buddy** in Settings Buddy. If a torn-off overlay was hidden, use the tray's **Show Buddy** action. - Drag Buddy itself out of the sidebar in the native Windows or macOS app. Browser/server and phone layouts cannot create the native overlay. - Use **Open full thread** for microphone controls, complex approvals, attachments, tool traces, and complete conversation history. - Restart Row-Bot to return Buddy placement to the sidebar dock; a saved hidden preference must still be turned back on.

# Home: Developer Home no longer has a Developer tab: a code folder now opens in its conversation's Developer panel. Read [Code Folders](/docs/developer/) for how to bind, clone and work on one.

## Home

Route: /docs/home/

Home's five tabs: Overview, Workflows, Knowledge, Monitor and Insights.

# Home Home is the start page for everything that isn't a single conversation. Choose **Home** in the sidebar, then one of its five tabs: - [Overview](/docs/home/overview) asks Row-Bot anything, lists what needs you, and shows live status and recent work. - [Workflows](/docs/home/workflows) lists saved workflows and reminders, runs them in one click, and opens the workflow editor. - [Knowledge](/docs/home/knowledge) shows the memory graph and the full memory library, with review, editing and Dream Cycle. - [Monitor](/docs/home/monitor) keeps the latest health checks with one-click fixes, plus activity, history and logs. - [Insights](/docs/home/insights) lists what Row-Bot noticed and the proposals it prepared for your review. Designs and code folders are not Home tabs: each opens in its conversation's panel. See [Designs](/docs/designer/) and [Code Folders](/docs/developer/). ## Full Guides - [Workflows guide](/docs/guides/workflows) - [Knowledge guide](/docs/knowledge/) - [Monitor guide](/docs/monitor/)

## Home: Knowledge

Route: /docs/home/knowledge

Use Home Knowledge to explore the memory graph, search and review memories, and run Dream Cycle.

# Home: Knowledge The Knowledge tab is where you see and manage what Row-Bot remembers: the memory graph, the full memory library, the review queue, recent recalls and changes, and Dream Cycle. ## What You Can Do Here - **Explore the graph.** It opens with up to 2,000 memories; **Show all** draws up to 5,000. - **Search and filter** the whole library by words or status, including the review queue. - **Open a memory** to see its details, connections, sources and when it was recalled. - **Add, edit, merge, archive, restore or delete** memories, one at a time or in bulk. Deleting is always reviewed first. - **Run Dream Cycle now** to tidy memory outside its overnight hours. Settings for remembering, graph health and the wiki vault are in **Settings Memory**. ## Next Step Open the [Knowledge guide](/docs/knowledge/) for the full walkthrough.

## Home: Monitor

Route: /docs/home/monitor

Use Home Monitor to see Row-Bot's latest health checks, fix problems in one click, and read activity, history and logs.

# Home: Monitor The Monitor tab answers: is everything healthy, what needs attention, and what happened recently? Row-Bot keeps the latest result of every check, so the tiles stay current after you switch tabs or restart. ## What You Can Do Here - **Needs attention** lists problems with a one-click fix, such as **Restart** a stopped channel or **Reconnect** an account. - **Health tiles** show each area's latest checks; open one for every check and its fix. - **Run diagnosis** runs every check now; **Copy diagnosis report** copies a summary for support. - **Check connections every hour** controls the checks that contact your providers, accounts and the internet. - **Activity**, **Maintenance**, **History** and **Logs** show what ran and why. ## Next Step Open the [Monitor guide](/docs/monitor/) for the full walkthrough.

## Home: Workflows

Route: /docs/home/workflows

Use Home Workflows to run saved workflows in one click, create or edit them on the page, and set delivery defaults.

# Home: Workflows The Workflows tab lists your saved workflows and reminders: when each runs next, how its last runs went, and what it is doing now. ## What You Can Do Here - **Run** starts a workflow at once; **Stop** appears while it runs. - **New workflow** and **Edit** open the workflow editor on this page. - **Enable** or **Disable** a workflow's schedule. - **Delivery defaults** choose the channels results are also sent to. - The **** menu on a row opens its run history, steps, settings or conversation, or duplicates or deletes it. ## Next Step Open the [Workflows guide](/docs/guides/workflows) for the full walkthrough.

## Reference Tables

Route: /docs/reference/generated/

Compact lookup tables for Row-Bot features and settings.

# Reference Tables

## Settings: Accounts

Route: /docs/settings/accounts

Settings no longer has an Accounts page; the GitHub, Google and X accounts are apps in Settings Apps.

# Settings: Accounts Settings no longer has an Accounts page. Your GitHub, Google and X accounts are apps now: open **Settings Apps** and choose **GitHub**, **Google** or **X**. On the app's page the account is a **Built in** way to connect, and **Set up** (or **Open** once it is set up) opens that one account's own settings: its setup guide, **Check**, **Reconnect** and **Disconnect**, and what Row-Bot may do with it. Read [Settings: Apps](/docs/settings/apps#built-in-ways-to-connect) and [Accounts And Authorisation](/docs/integrations/accounts). Old Accounts links open the matching app in Row-Bot.

## Settings: Channels

Route: /docs/settings/channels

Settings no longer has a Channels page; Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack and SMS are apps in Settings Apps.

# Settings: Channels Settings no longer has a Channels page. Each channel is an app now: open **Settings Apps** and choose **Telegram**, **WhatsApp**, **Discord**, **Slack** or **Text messages** (SMS); the **Communication** category lists them together. On the app's page the channel is a **Built in** way to connect, and **Set up** (or **Open** once it is set up) opens that one channel's own settings: its connect steps, **Start** and **Stop**, pairing, and paired accounts. Read [Settings: Apps](/docs/settings/apps#built-in-ways-to-connect) and [Channels](/docs/integrations/channels). Old Channels links open the matching app in Row-Bot, or the Communication apps when they named no channel.

## Settings: Integrations

Route: /docs/settings/integrations

Settings no longer has an Integrations page; apps are in Settings Apps and skills are in Settings Skills.

# Settings: Integrations Settings no longer has an Integrations page. What it held now lives on two pages: - Services Row-Bot can work in, packages, catalogs and custom connections: **Settings Apps**. Read [Settings: Apps](/docs/settings/apps). - Skills: **Settings Skills**. Read [Settings: Skills](/docs/settings/skills). Old Integrations links open the matching page in Row-Bot.

## Settings: MCP

Route: /docs/settings/mcp

Settings no longer has an MCP page; connections are apps in Settings Apps.

# Settings: MCP Settings no longer has an MCP page. MCP connections are apps in **Settings Apps**; catalogs, runtimes, **Apps in chats** and **Add a custom connection** are under **Apps Advanced**. Read [Settings: Apps](/docs/settings/apps) and [MCP](/docs/integrations/mcp). Old MCP links open the matching place in Row-Bot.

## Settings: Plugins

Route: /docs/settings/plugins

Settings no longer has a Plugins page; packages are in Settings Apps.

# Settings: Plugins Settings no longer has a Plugins page. Packages are added, turned off and removed in **Settings Apps**, and the apps and skills a package brings show **Installed as part of _package_**. Read [Settings: Apps](/docs/settings/apps) and [Plugins](/docs/integrations/plugins). Old Plugins links open the matching place in Row-Bot.

## Settings: Utilities

Route: /docs/settings/utilities

Settings no longer has a Utilities page; the built-in tools are part of Settings Tools.

# Settings: Utilities The built-in tools that used to live under Utilities are now in **Settings Tools Built-in tools**. Read [Settings: Tools](/docs/settings/tools).

## UI Tour

Route: /docs/ui-tour/

A short guided tour of Row-Bot: the sidebar, Home, a conversation, panels, the command palette and Settings.

# UI Tour Use this short tour if you want the quickest mental map before reading detailed pages. 1. Start with the [Row-Bot Interface](/docs/app-shell/navigation): the sidebar, Home, a conversation and its details card, panels, the terminal, and the K command palette. 2. Read [Home: Overview](/docs/home/overview), the first page Row-Bot opens: the Ask box, what needs you, live status and recent work. 3. Read [Chat](/docs/chat/) for conversations, the composer, models, attachments, tool traces and approvals. 4. See how a conversation works on a design or code folder in [Designs](/docs/designer/) and [Code Folders](/docs/developer/). 5. Open [Settings](/docs/settings/) when you are ready to connect providers, choose models, and set up memory, tools, apps (your accounts and channels included) and devices. 6. Keep [Privacy And Safety](/docs/privacy-safety/) nearby when enabling external services or action tools.
